bio.q: Hexokinase catalyzes the very first step of glycolysis: glucose + ATP → glucose-6-phosphate + ADP. This step is highly exergonic (ΔG ≈ −16.7 kJ/mol) and is considered functionally irreversible under cellular conditions. Why is this step physiologically important?
opts: Because the cell lacks any enzyme that can reverse it
Because the strongly negative ΔG ensures unidirectional flow and traps glucose inside the cell as glucose-6-phosphate (which cannot leave via GLUT transporters), committing it to glycolysis
Because it requires two ATPs rather than one
Because it produces ATP rather than consuming it
Because hexokinase has no allosteric regulation
bio.why: Hexokinase is functionally irreversible because the ΔG is large and negative. Phosphorylation also traps glucose: G6P is charged and cannot diffuse out via GLUT transporters, committing the molecule to glycolysis. Cells reverse the step (during gluconeogenesis) using a different enzyme, glucose-6-phosphatase, present mainly in liver and kidney.

bio.q: During intense exercise, skeletal muscle outpaces oxygen delivery. Glycolysis continues at high rate, producing pyruvate and NADH, but mitochondrial respiration cannot keep up. Lactate fermentation kicks in: pyruvate is reduced to lactate by lactate dehydrogenase. What is the primary purpose of this conversion?
opts: To generate additional ATP from pyruvate
To regenerate NAD+ from NADH so glycolysis can continue (otherwise NAD+ would be depleted, halting the GAPDH step)
To produce pyruvate from amino acids during fasting
bio.why: Glycolysis depletes NAD+ rapidly at the GAPDH step (NAD+ → NADH). Without aerobic respiration to reoxidize NADH, glycolysis would halt within seconds. Lactate fermentation regenerates NAD+ by transferring electrons from NADH to pyruvate, allowing glycolysis to continue producing 2 ATP per glucose anaerobically.

bio.q: One molecule of glucose enters glycolysis and is converted to 2 molecules of pyruvate. Each pyruvate enters the mitochondrial matrix, is decarboxylated by pyruvate dehydrogenase to acetyl-CoA, and the acetyl group enters the citric acid cycle. How many TIMES does the Krebs cycle run per glucose molecule?
opts: Once — one glucose generates one acetyl-CoA
Twice — one glucose produces two pyruvate, each becoming one acetyl-CoA, each running the cycle once
Four times, since each pyruvate runs the cycle twice
Depends on oxygen availability — the cycle runs more times in low oxygen
Six times, once per carbon in glucose
bio.why: Glucose (6 carbons) → 2 pyruvate (3 carbons each) → 2 acetyl-CoA (2 carbons each, releasing 2 CO₂). Each acetyl-CoA enters the cycle once, so the cycle runs TWICE per glucose. Total per glucose: 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ + 2 ATP/GTP + 4 CO₂ from the Krebs steps alone.

bio.q: Cyanide poisoning causes rapid cellular death because it binds with high affinity to a specific component of the electron transport chain, preventing electrons from being transferred to molecular oxygen. The result is a complete halt of oxidative phosphorylation. Which complex does cyanide inhibit?
opts: Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase), inhibited by rotenone instead
Complex III (cytochrome bc1), inhibited by antimycin A instead
Complex IV (cytochrome c oxidase), the terminal electron acceptor that transfers electrons to O₂
ATP synthase, which is inhibited by oligomycin
bio.why: Cyanide binds the iron in cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), preventing electrons from reaching molecular oxygen. The whole ETC backs up, ATP production halts, and cells switch to glycolysis (insufficient ATP). Carbon monoxide acts at the same site. Rotenone hits Complex I; antimycin A hits Complex III; oligomycin blocks ATP synthase.

bio.q: 2,4-Dinitrophenol (DNP) is a small lipid-soluble molecule that can carry protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane, dissipating the proton gradient established by the ETC. The ETC continues to run (electrons still reach O₂), but ATP synthesis collapses. Excess oxidized NADH energy is released as heat. What is DNP classified as?
opts: An ETC inhibitor that blocks electron flow
An uncoupler — it dissipates the proton gradient, separating (uncoupling) the ETC from ATP synthesis; energy is released as heat instead of chemical bonds
An ATP synthase activator that boosts ATP production
A Krebs-cycle inhibitor that blocks decarboxylation
An NAD+ regenerator that bypasses lactate fermentation
bio.why: DNP (and related uncouplers like FCCP, plus the natural uncoupling protein UCP1 in brown adipose) carry protons across the inner membrane, collapsing the gradient. The ETC keeps oxidizing NADH but ATP synthase has no driving force — energy escapes as heat. Brown fat uses this physiologically for non-shivering thermogenesis.

bio.q: When all major pathways of cellular respiration (glycolysis, pyruvate decarboxylation, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain, oxidative phosphorylation) are accounted for under modern P/O ratio estimates (NADH ~2.5 ATP, FADH₂ ~1.5 ATP), what is the approximate net ATP yield per glucose?
opts: ~10 ATP, comparable to anaerobic glycolysis alone
~30-32 ATP, the modern estimate (older textbooks reported ~36-38 using P/O of 3 and 2)
~50 ATP, if every electron made one ATP
bio.why: Modern estimates: glycolysis 2 ATP + 2 NADH (cytoplasmic), pyruvate dec. 2 NADH, Krebs 6 NADH + 2 FADH₂ + 2 GTP per glucose. Using P/O ratios of 2.5 (NADH) and 1.5 (FADH₂), net yield is ~30-32 ATP. Older texts used 3 and 2, giving ~36-38. Cytoplasmic NADH may use the glycerol shuttle (loses 1 ATP each).

bio.q: Photosystem II uses light energy to split water in a unique reaction: 2 H₂O → 4 H⁺ + 4 e⁻ + O₂. The electrons replace those that have been excited and passed down the photosynthetic electron transport chain. The protons accumulate in the thylakoid lumen, contributing to the proton gradient. What is the principal product released to the atmosphere from this water-splitting step?
opts: O₂ — molecular oxygen, regenerated as a 'waste' product of photolysis
NADPH, the reducing power for the Calvin cycle
Glucose, the end product of photosynthesis
ATP, generated by chloroplast ATP synthase
bio.why: Water photolysis at PSII generates O₂ as a byproduct. This is the source of nearly all atmospheric oxygen. The electrons replace those excited by light at PSII; the protons add to the thylakoid lumen gradient. NADPH is generated downstream (at PSI/ferredoxin/NADP⁺ reductase); ATP is made by chloroplast ATP synthase.

bio.q: The Calvin cycle in chloroplasts fixes CO₂ into a 5-carbon sugar (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate, RuBP), forming an unstable 6-carbon intermediate that immediately splits into two 3-carbon molecules. The enzyme catalyzing this carboxylation is the most abundant protein on Earth. Which enzyme is it?
opts: Hexokinase, the first enzyme of glycolysis
RuBisCO (ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase) — the most abundant protein on Earth, fixing CO₂ at the entry of the Calvin cycle
Phosphofructokinase-1, the regulatory step of glycolysis
ATP synthase, used in both chloroplasts and mitochondria
Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxylase, used in C4 photosynthesis
bio.why: RuBisCO catalyzes CO₂ fixation onto RuBP — the entry step of the Calvin cycle. It accounts for roughly half of all soluble protein in plant leaves and is considered the most abundant protein on Earth. It also has a side activity (oxygenase, leading to photorespiration), which is why C4 and CAM plants have evolved to minimize this.

bio.q: Hot, sunny climates increase the oxygenase activity of RuBisCO (photorespiration) which wastes carbon and energy. C4 plants such as corn and sugarcane have evolved a specialized anatomy and biochemistry to minimize this. How do C4 plants suppress photorespiration?
opts: By directly inhibiting RuBisCO with a small-molecule inhibitor
By spatially separating CO₂ capture (by PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells) from CO₂ fixation (by RuBisCO in bundle-sheath cells), where local CO₂ is concentrated and outcompetes O₂
By closing stomata permanently to exclude O₂
By performing photosynthesis only at night (CAM strategy)
By abandoning the Calvin cycle entirely
bio.why: C4 plants use PEP carboxylase (no O₂ side reaction) in mesophyll cells to fix CO₂ into oxaloacetate. This 4-carbon molecule travels to the bundle-sheath cells, where decarboxylation releases CO₂ at high local concentration around RuBisCO. The high CO₂:O₂ ratio suppresses RuBisCO's oxygenase activity, minimizing photorespiration.

bio.q: CAM (crassulacean acid metabolism) plants — typified by cacti and succulents — open their stomata only at night to conserve water in arid environments. They fix CO₂ at night using PEP carboxylase, store the carbon as malate in the vacuole, and release CO₂ into the Calvin cycle during the day. What is the primary advantage of this strategy?
opts: Fixes CO₂ at night and stores it; daytime stomatal closure prevents water loss while CO₂ is released to the Calvin cycle from stored malate
Stores additional water in the leaf overnight
Doubles ATP yield compared to C3 plants
bio.why: CAM plants temporally separate CO₂ uptake (night, stomata open) from carbon fixation (day, stomata closed). Nocturnal CO₂ is fixed by PEP carboxylase to oxaloacetate → malate, stored in vacuoles. During day, malate releases CO₂ to RuBisCO. Closing stomata during hot days dramatically reduces water loss — critical in arid habitats.

bio.q: After DNA replication in S phase, each chromosome consists of two identical sister chromatids held together along their length, with the strongest attachment at the centromere. A multiprotein complex physically clamps the sister chromatids together until anaphase, when it is cleaved by separase. Which protein complex is this?
opts: The kinetochore, which attaches chromosomes to microtubules
Cohesin, a ring-shaped complex that holds sister chromatids together along their entire length until anaphase
Lamins, which form the nuclear lamina
bio.why: Cohesin is a ring-shaped protein complex that physically encircles sister chromatids, holding them together from S phase until anaphase. At the metaphase-anaphase transition, the spindle assembly checkpoint is satisfied and separase cleaves cohesin, allowing sisters to separate. Condensin compacts chromosomes (a separate role).

bio.q: During mitosis, replicated chromosomes (each consisting of two sister chromatids) undergo a precisely orchestrated series of movements directed by the spindle apparatus. There is a specific phase in which all chromosomes are aligned along the equator of the cell, with each centromere attached to spindle fibers from BOTH poles. Which phase is this?
opts: Prophase, when chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope dissolves
Metaphase, when chromosomes align at the metaphase plate (cell equator), each attached to spindle fibers from both poles via kinetochores
Anaphase, when sister chromatids separate and migrate to opposite poles
Telophase, when nuclear envelopes reform around the daughter nuclei
Cytokinesis, when the cytoplasm physically divides
bio.why: Metaphase is defined by chromosome alignment at the metaphase plate. Each sister chromatid pair attaches to spindle fibers from both poles (bi-orientation). Only when all chromosomes are bi-oriented and tension is sensed does the spindle assembly checkpoint allow progression to anaphase.

bio.q: A transcription factor encoded by the TP53 gene is upregulated in response to DNA damage. It activates downstream genes that arrest the cell cycle (e.g., p21, a CDK inhibitor) or trigger apoptosis if the damage cannot be repaired. Mutation of this gene is found in over half of human cancers. By what nickname is this protein known?
opts: A cyclin, the regulatory subunit of CDK complexes
A CDK (cyclin-dependent kinase), the catalytic subunit of cell-cycle drivers
The 'guardian of the genome' — p53, a tumor suppressor that arrests the cell cycle or triggers apoptosis in response to DNA damage
A histone, the protein that packages DNA
bio.why: p53 (TP53 protein) is famously called the 'guardian of the genome.' It is activated by DNA damage and other stresses; downstream, it transcribes p21 (a CDK inhibitor that arrests the cell cycle at G1/S) and apoptosis genes (BAX, PUMA). Loss of p53 function is one of the most common alterations in human cancers.

bio.q: Animal cells divide their cytoplasm at the end of mitosis through formation of a contractile ring of actin and myosin that pinches the cell in half (cleavage furrow). Plant cells, surrounded by a rigid cell wall, cannot pinch and instead use a different mechanism. How do plant cells complete cytokinesis?
opts: By forming a cleavage furrow with actin/myosin, identical to animal cells
By assembling a cell plate at the cell equator from vesicles delivered along microtubules; vesicles fuse to form a new cell wall and plasma membrane between daughter cells
By assembling a new spindle that mechanically separates the cytoplasm
By forming a septum from mitochondrial-derived membrane
By extruding excess cytoplasm through a single pore
bio.why: Plant cytokinesis uses a cell plate, not a cleavage furrow. Microtubules deliver Golgi-derived vesicles to the cell equator. Vesicles fuse to form a new plasma membrane and cell wall between the daughter cells. The cell plate grows outward until it fuses with the existing cell wall, completing division.

bio.q: Telomeres are repetitive DNA sequences (TTAGGG in vertebrates) at chromosome ends that shorten slightly with each replication cycle. Cells with long-term proliferative potential maintain telomere length using a specific reverse-transcriptase enzyme that carries its own RNA template. In which cell types is this telomerase enzyme MOST highly expressed?
opts: Differentiated somatic cells — stable, fully matured tissues
Stem cells, germline cells, and ~90% of cancer cells — populations that need long-term proliferation
Bacteria, which use telomerase to seal circular chromosomes
Red blood cells, which have no nucleus
bio.why: Telomerase is highly expressed in stem cells (for self-renewal), germline cells (transmitting full-length telomeres to offspring), and most cancer cells (~90%, which need to bypass replicative senescence). Most differentiated somatic cells repress telomerase, so telomeres shorten with each division — eventually triggering senescence (Hayflick limit).

bio.q: DNA polymerase III in E. coli has very high fidelity (~1 error per 10⁷ bases) thanks to base-selectivity at the active site PLUS a built-in proofreading function. If a wrong nucleotide is incorporated, the polymerase backs up, removes the misincorporated base, and re-polymerizes. Which catalytic activity drives this proofreading?
opts: 5' → 3' exonuclease activity, also used to remove RNA primers
3' → 5' exonuclease activity, an intrinsic proofreading function that excises mispaired bases at the 3' end of the growing strand
Helicase activity, used to separate strands
Endonuclease activity, used to introduce double-strand breaks
Reverse transcriptase activity, found only in retroviruses
bio.why: DNA polymerase III has 3' → 5' exonuclease activity in a separate domain. When a wrong base is incorporated, the resulting mispairing distorts the active site; the polymerase moves the 3' end into the exonuclease site, removes the wrong nucleotide, and resumes synthesis. This proofreading lowers the error rate ~100-fold beyond base selectivity alone.

bio.q: DNA replication is bidirectional: at each replication fork, one strand is synthesized continuously (leading strand) while the other is synthesized as short fragments (Okazaki fragments) that are later joined. The reason for this asymmetry is intrinsic to the directionality of DNA polymerase. Why does the lagging strand REQUIRE Okazaki fragments?
opts: A different polymerase synthesizes the lagging strand

DNA polymerase can only synthesize 5' → 3', but the parental DNA strands are antiparallel — so the template for the lagging strand runs the wrong way for continuous synthesis. Short fragments are made backwards from the fork.
The lagging strand uses a slower polymerase
There is no primer available for continuous lagging-strand synthesis
The lagging strand is composed of RNA, not DNA
bio.why: DNA polymerase only synthesizes 5' → 3'. At a replication fork, one parental strand has its 3' end pointing toward the fork (leading template, continuous synthesis); the other has its 3' end pointing AWAY from the fork (lagging template). Synthesis of the lagging strand must proceed away from the fork in short bursts, each starting from a primer — the Okazaki fragments — which are later joined by ligase.

bio.q: Eukaryotic cells contain three nuclear RNA polymerases that transcribe distinct classes of genes. One specific polymerase synthesizes pre-mRNAs from protein-coding genes, while the other two transcribe rRNA and tRNA respectively. Which polymerase produces eukaryotic mRNA?
opts: RNA polymerase I — transcribes large rRNA genes (28S, 18S, 5.8S) in the nucleolus
RNA polymerase II — transcribes protein-coding genes into pre-mRNA, plus most snRNAs and miRNAs
RNA polymerase III — transcribes tRNAs, 5S rRNA, and small RNAs
DNA polymerase, which copies DNA, not RNA
Mitochondrial RNA polymerase, which only transcribes mitochondrial genes
bio.why: RNA Pol II transcribes protein-coding genes into pre-mRNA. Pol I makes large rRNA in the nucleolus; Pol III makes tRNAs and 5S rRNA. The Pol II C-terminal domain (CTD) coordinates capping, splicing, and polyadenylation, distinguishing mRNA biogenesis from other RNA classes.

bio.q: Approximately 25-35 nucleotides upstream of the transcription start site, many eukaryotic protein-coding genes contain a conserved sequence rich in adenine and thymine. The TATA-binding protein (TBP, part of TFIID) recognizes this sequence to position RNA polymerase II. Where is the TATA box located relative to the gene?
opts: Within the coding sequence, in the middle of an exon
In the core promoter, upstream of the transcription start site, where it positions the pre-initiation complex
In the terminator, where transcription stops
Only in the 5' untranslated region of the mature mRNA
In an enhancer thousands of base pairs away from the gene
bio.why: The TATA box is a core-promoter element ~25 bp upstream of the transcription start site. TBP binds the AT-rich sequence and bends the DNA, recruiting other general transcription factors and RNA Pol II. Not all genes have a TATA box; some use alternative core elements (e.g., TATA-less CpG-island promoters).

bio.q: After RNA polymerase II transcribes a eukaryotic gene, the pre-mRNA contains both protein-coding sequences and intervening non-coding sequences. A large ribonucleoprotein machine recognizes specific sequences at intron-exon boundaries (5' GU and 3' AG splice sites) and removes the non-coding regions, ligating the protein-coding pieces. What does the spliceosome remove?
opts: Exons (protein-coding sequences) that interrupt regulatory regions
Introns — non-coding intervening sequences — leaving the exons joined
The poly-A tail at the 3' end of the mRNA
The 5' methylguanosine cap added during transcription
bio.why: The spliceosome (a complex of snRNPs U1, U2, U4, U5, U6) excises introns and joins exons. Splice sites are marked by GU at the 5' splice site and AG at the 3' splice site. Alternative splicing (using different exon combinations) lets one gene produce multiple protein isoforms — vastly expanding proteome diversity.

bio.q: After eukaryotic transcription terminates, ~150-250 adenine residues are enzymatically added to the 3' end of the pre-mRNA by poly(A) polymerase. This poly(A) tail is bound by poly(A)-binding proteins (PABP) and serves multiple functions in mRNA biology. Which is the PRIMARY function of the poly(A) tail?
opts: Translation initiation by directly binding ribosomes
mRNA stability (protects from 3' exonucleases) and nuclear export, plus enhanced translation efficiency through PABP-eIF4G circularization
Direct ribosome binding through codon-anticodon pairing
Splicing of introns from the pre-mRNA
Encoding the C-terminus of the encoded protein
bio.why: The poly(A) tail protects mRNA from 3' → 5' exonucleases, is required for nuclear export, and enhances translation by recruiting PABP, which interacts with the eIF4G/cap complex to circularize the mRNA — increasing ribosome reinitiation. Tail shortening (deadenylation) is a major signal for mRNA decay.

bio.q: When a small ribosomal subunit scans an mRNA from the 5' cap looking for the start of translation, it identifies a specific codon to initiate protein synthesis. This codon also codes for the first amino acid of every protein (later cleaved in many cases). Which mRNA codon is the universal start codon?
opts: AUG, which codes for methionine (formyl-methionine in prokaryotes) and is the universal start codon
GUG, used as an alternative start in some bacterial genes (rare)
UAA, one of the three stop codons
bio.why: AUG is the universal start codon. It pairs with the special initiator tRNA carrying methionine (in eukaryotes) or N-formyl-methionine (in prokaryotes). Some bacteria use GUG as an alternate start, but AUG is dominant. Internal AUGs encode methionine in the elongation phase.

bio.q: The ribosome catalyzes peptide bond formation between the carboxyl end of a growing polypeptide (in the P site) and the amino group of an incoming aminoacyl-tRNA (in the A site). The catalytic activity is NOT performed by a protein but by an RNA molecule. Where in the ribosome does peptide bond formation occur?
opts: By a protein enzyme called peptidyl transferase
By the rRNA in the large ribosomal subunit (the peptidyl transferase center) — the ribosome is a ribozyme; the rRNA does the chemistry
By mRNA in the small subunit
By the ribosomal exit tunnel (E site)
bio.why: The ribosome is a ribozyme. The peptidyl transferase active site in the large subunit is composed entirely of rRNA (no protein side chains involved in catalysis). This was a major piece of evidence for the RNA World hypothesis — that ancient catalysis was RNA-based before proteins took over most enzymatic functions.

bio.q: Crick's wobble hypothesis explains how 61 sense codons can be read by fewer than 61 different tRNA species. The first two codon positions pair stringently (Watson-Crick), while the third position allows non-standard pairing — for example, inosine in tRNA can pair with U, C, or A. Which codon position shows wobble?
opts: 1st codon position (5' end), which is fully redundant
2nd codon position, where U can pair with G
3rd codon position (3' end of the codon, 5' end of the anticodon), where non-standard pairing allows one tRNA to read multiple codons
Anticodon center (middle of the tRNA), which has no role in pairing
bio.why: Wobble occurs at the 3rd codon position, which pairs with the 5' (first) position of the anticodon. Modified bases like inosine here can pair with multiple bases (U, C, A), so one tRNA can recognize several codons coding for the same amino acid. This explains the observed redundancy of the genetic code.

bio.q: When a protein destined for secretion (e.g., insulin, antibody) is being translated, a short hydrophobic sequence near the N-terminus is recognized by the signal recognition particle (SRP). SRP halts translation and brings the ribosome to a specific organelle, where translation resumes and the polypeptide is threaded into the lumen. Where is the ribosome directed?
opts: Mitochondrion, where signal sequences direct matrix proteins
Rough endoplasmic reticulum, where the signal peptide is recognized by the Sec61 translocon and the polypeptide enters the ER lumen
Cytoplasm, where free ribosomes translate cytosolic proteins
bio.why: Signal peptides direct ribosomes to the rough ER. SRP binds the signal sequence as it emerges from the ribosome and brings the complex to the SRP receptor on the ER membrane. The Sec61 translocon then channels the polypeptide co-translationally into the ER lumen, where signal peptidase cleaves the signal peptide. Mitochondrial, nuclear, and peroxisomal proteins use post-translational targeting via different signals.

bio.q: A point mutation is a change at a single nucleotide position in a gene. Depending on which codon and how the resulting protein is affected, the consequence varies dramatically. Which set of outcome categories accurately describes the possible effects of a point mutation in a coding region?
opts: Always silent — no effect because of code redundancy
Silent (no amino-acid change), missense (different amino acid), or nonsense (premature stop codon)
Always frameshift, since one nucleotide alters the reading frame
Always splice-site changes, regardless of codon
bio.why: A single nucleotide substitution can be (a) silent — wobble-position change with no amino-acid change; (b) missense — different amino acid encoded; or (c) nonsense — substitution to a stop codon, truncating the protein. Frameshift mutations result from insertions or deletions, not single substitutions.

bio.q: Sickle-cell disease is caused by a single nucleotide change in the β-globin gene that converts an A to a T at the second codon position. The result is a substitution of glutamate (Glu, GAG) by valine (Val, GTG) at position 6 of the β-globin chain — a single amino-acid change with profound clinical consequences. What type of mutation is this?
opts: Frameshift mutation, shifting the reading frame downstream
Silent mutation, with no amino-acid change
Missense mutation — Glu → Val at β-globin position 6, changing one amino acid
Nonsense mutation, creating a premature stop codon
bio.why: Sickle-cell is the textbook missense mutation. A single A→T substitution changes Glu (acidic, charged) to Val (hydrophobic) at position 6 of β-globin. The resulting hydrophobic surface patch causes hemoglobin to polymerize when deoxygenated, distorting RBCs into a sickle shape — driving anemia, vaso-occlusion, and pain crises.

bio.q: DNA point mutations are categorized into two types based on how the substitution affects the chemical class of the base. One type substitutes within the same chemical family (e.g., A↔G), while the other type swaps between families. Which definition correctly distinguishes these two types?
opts: Transition and transversion are interchangeable terms with no real distinction
Transition = purine ↔ purine (A↔G) or pyrimidine ↔ pyrimidine (C↔T); transversion = purine ↔ pyrimidine (e.g., A↔C). Transitions are more common since they are easier chemically
Transversion = always silent; transition = always missense
Both create stop codons by definition
Transition affects only RNA; transversion affects only DNA
bio.why: Transition is a purine→purine or pyrimidine→pyrimidine substitution (chemically similar). Transversion is purine→pyrimidine (or vice versa) — a bigger structural change. Transitions outnumber transversions about 2:1 because they are easier to make (similar ring structure makes mispairing easier during replication).

bio.q: Just after replication, occasional mismatched bases (A paired with C, for example) escape the polymerase's proofreading. A specialized DNA repair pathway then identifies the newly synthesized strand (which contains the error), excises a short patch around the mismatch, and resynthesizes correctly. Which type of damage does mismatch repair primarily fix?
opts: UV-induced thymine dimers, removed by nucleotide excision repair
Base mispairs that escape proofreading immediately after DNA replication
Double-strand breaks, repaired by homologous recombination or non-homologous end joining
DNA methylation marks, which are not damage at all
bio.why: Mismatch repair targets base-base mispairs and small insertion/deletion loops left after DNA replication. In E. coli, MutS recognizes the mismatch, MutL/MutH cleave the unmethylated (newly synthesized) strand, and a polymerase + ligase complete the repair. Inherited mutations in MMR genes (MSH2, MLH1) cause Lynch syndrome (hereditary colon cancer).

bio.q: Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum (XP) develop severe sun-induced skin damage and dramatically elevated skin-cancer risk. Their cells are unable to repair UV-induced thymine dimers, which then cause replication errors and mutations. XP is caused by a defect in which DNA repair pathway?
opts: Base excision repair (BER), which fixes oxidized or alkylated bases
Nucleotide excision repair (NER), which removes bulky lesions like UV-induced thymine dimers by excising a short oligonucleotide
DNA polymerase III, which synthesizes new DNA strands
Mismatch repair, which fixes post-replication errors
bio.why: Xeroderma pigmentosum is caused by mutations in NER genes (XPA-XPG). NER recognizes bulky helix-distorting lesions like UV-induced thymine dimers (cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers), excises a ~25-30 nt oligonucleotide containing the lesion, and resynthesizes. Without NER, dimers persist and cause mutations during replication.

bio.q: The lac operon in E. coli contains three structural genes (lacZ, lacY, lacA) for lactose metabolism, plus a regulatory gene encoding a tetrameric protein that binds the operator and blocks transcription in the absence of lactose. Which gene encodes the lac repressor?
opts: lacZ — encodes β-galactosidase, the enzyme that cleaves lactose
lacI — the regulatory gene encoding the tetrameric Lac repressor protein, located upstream of the operon
lacY — encodes lactose permease, which imports lactose into the cell
lacA — encodes thiogalactoside transacetylase, of secondary importance
The CAP-binding site, which is a regulatory DNA sequence (not a gene)
bio.why: lacI is the regulatory gene encoding the Lac repressor (a tetrameric protein). When lactose is absent, the repressor binds the operator and blocks transcription. When allolactose (an isomer of lactose) is present, it binds the repressor and removes it from DNA, allowing transcription. lacZ, lacY, lacA are the structural genes.

bio.q: The lac operon is positively regulated by catabolite activator protein (CAP, also called CRP), which binds DNA only when complexed with cyclic AMP (cAMP). Glucose levels modulate cAMP via inverse regulation of adenylate cyclase. When does CAP-cAMP bind the lac promoter and activate transcription?
opts: When glucose is HIGH (lots of preferred energy source available)
When glucose is LOW — low glucose causes cAMP to rise (no glucose-inhibition of adenylate cyclase), and CAP-cAMP then activates the lac promoter, allowing lactose use as a backup energy source
Glucose levels do not affect CAP function
Only when glucose and lactose are both equal in concentration
bio.why: Glucose suppresses cAMP via catabolite repression. When glucose is LOW, cAMP rises, binds CAP, and CAP-cAMP binds the lac promoter to recruit RNA polymerase. This means the lac operon is expressed only when (1) lactose is present (repressor off) AND (2) glucose is low (CAP-cAMP on) — the cell uses glucose first.

bio.q: Histone tail acetylation by histone acetyltransferases (HATs) such as p300/CBP transfers acetyl groups to lysine residues. The chemical effect is to neutralize the positive charge on lysine, weakening the histone-DNA interaction. What is the typical effect of histone acetylation on gene expression?
opts: Silences transcription by tightly compacting chromatin
Activates transcription by neutralizing histone positive charges, loosening DNA-histone contacts (open chromatin), and recruiting bromodomain-containing transcriptional activators
Has no effect on chromatin or transcription
bio.why: Histone acetylation neutralizes lysine positive charges, weakening histone-DNA interactions and opening chromatin (euchromatin). Acetylated histones are also bound by bromodomain proteins (e.g., BRD4) that recruit transcriptional machinery. Histone deacetylases (HDACs) reverse this and silence genes; HDAC inhibitors are used as anticancer drugs.

bio.q: DNA methylation in mammals primarily targets cytosines within CpG dinucleotides, especially those clustered in 'CpG islands' near gene promoters. Methyl-CpG-binding proteins (e.g., MeCP2) and chromatin remodelers then assemble repressive chromatin structures. What is the typical effect of CpG-island methylation at a gene promoter?
opts: Activates transcription by recruiting RNA polymerase
Silences transcription — methylated promoters are bound by repressive factors and assemble closed chromatin
Causes mutation by directly damaging the DNA backbone
Promotes splicing by marking exon-intron boundaries
bio.why: CpG-island methylation (5-methylcytosine in promoter regions) silences gene expression. Methyl-CpG-binding proteins recruit histone deacetylases and other repressors, compacting chromatin. Aberrant promoter hypermethylation silences tumor suppressors in cancer; X-inactivation and genomic imprinting also use this mechanism.

bio.q: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are short ~22-nucleotide non-coding RNAs that, after processing, are loaded into the RISC complex and guide the complex to complementary sites typically in the 3' UTR of target mRNAs. By what mechanism do miRNAs regulate gene expression?
opts: By methylating cytosines in DNA (epigenetic silencing)
By base-pairing with target mRNAs and either accelerating their decay (perfect pairing) or blocking translation (imperfect pairing) via the RISC complex
By acetylating histones at target gene promoters
By splicing pre-mRNA into mature mRNA
By directly binding RNA polymerase II and inhibiting transcription
bio.why: miRNAs base-pair with sites in the 3' UTR (or other regions) of target mRNAs. The miRNA-RISC complex either cleaves the target mRNA (if pairing is near-perfect, plant-like) or represses translation and accelerates deadenylation (mammalian, imperfect pairing). One miRNA can target hundreds of mRNAs, so they sit at major regulatory hubs (e.g., let-7, miR-21).

bio.q: A clinical microbiology laboratory uses Gram staining to differentiate two major bacterial groups. Gram-positive bacteria stain purple/violet, while Gram-negative bacteria appear pink after counterstaining. The difference reflects fundamental cell-wall architecture. What is the structural distinction?
opts: Gram-positive: thick peptidoglycan wall, no outer membrane. Gram-negative: thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane with lipopolysaccharide (LPS, which is endotoxic)
Different ribosome size — 70S in one, 80S in the other
Different plasma membrane composition (cholesterol vs no cholesterol)
Both have identical cell walls but different cytoplasmic pH
bio.why: Gram-positive bacteria have a single thick peptidoglycan cell wall (retains crystal violet → purple). Gram-negative bacteria have a thin peptidoglycan layer between an inner plasma membrane and an outer membrane containing LPS (lose crystal violet → counterstain pink). LPS is the endotoxin responsible for septic shock; the outer membrane also makes Gram-negative bacteria more antibiotic-resistant.

bio.q: Some bacteria (e.g., Bacillus, Clostridium) survive harsh environmental conditions by forming highly resistant dormant structures. These structures contain dehydrated cytoplasm, a thick protein coat, and DPA-Ca²⁺ in their core, allowing them to withstand boiling, desiccation, and UV radiation for years. What are these structures called?
opts: Bacterial endospores — dormant, highly resistant survival forms produced inside the parent cell during nutrient deprivation
Viral particles released during lytic infection
Capsule polysaccharide layers around growing cells
bio.why: Endospores are formed within the parent cell in response to starvation. The DPA-Ca²⁺ core, multiple protein coats, and dehydrated cytoplasm make endospores extraordinarily resistant — Clostridium botulinum spores survive boiling. Pressure-cooking (autoclaving at 121°C) is required to kill them. Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) spreads via these durable spores.

bio.q: Eukaryotic cilia and flagella have a strikingly conserved internal structure. A cross-section under TEM reveals a characteristic arrangement of microtubule doublets surrounding a central pair, anchored to a basal body. Which microtubule arrangement defines this axoneme?
opts: 9+0 — nine outer doublets, no central pair (found in primary, non-motile cilia)
9+2 — nine outer microtubule DOUBLETS arranged around 2 central singlets (motile cilia and flagella)
9+1 — nine outer doublets, one central singlet
8+2 — eight outer doublets and two central singlets
bio.why: Motile cilia and flagella have a 9+2 axoneme: nine outer microtubule doublets around two central singlets. Dynein motor arms on the doublets generate movement by sliding adjacent doublets relative to one another. Primary (non-motile) cilia have a 9+0 arrangement and serve sensory functions (e.g., Hedgehog signaling).

bio.q: Bacterial flagella propel cells through liquid environments and look superficially similar to eukaryotic flagella. However, their molecular architecture and energy source are fundamentally different. Which statement correctly distinguishes bacterial from eukaryotic flagella?
opts: Both have the same axoneme structure and use the same propulsion mechanism

Bacterial flagella are made of flagellin protein, are hollow filaments anchored to a rotary motor, and are driven by a proton (or sodium) gradient — not ATP. Eukaryotic flagella are 9+2 microtubule axonemes that bend using dynein-driven sliding powered by ATP.
Bacterial flagella are powered by ATP hydrolysis like eukaryotic flagella
Eukaryotic flagella are simpler than bacterial flagella
bio.why: Bacterial flagella are structurally and energetically distinct: they are flagellin polymers anchored to a rotary motor in the cell envelope, powered by the proton motive force (H+ flow drives rotation). Eukaryotic flagella are 9+2 axonemes built from microtubules; dynein motors, fueled by ATP, slide microtubules to generate bending.

bio.q: Cholesterol intercalates between phospholipids in animal cell membranes and modulates membrane fluidity in a temperature-dependent manner. At high temperatures it restrains phospholipid movement; at low temperatures it disrupts ordered packing. Which statement best summarizes cholesterol's effect?
opts: Cholesterol always increases fluidity, regardless of temperature
Cholesterol always decreases fluidity, regardless of temperature
Cholesterol BUFFERS fluidity — it increases fluidity at low temperatures (preventing rigid crystallization) and decreases fluidity at high temperatures (preventing excessive disorder)
Cholesterol has no measurable effect on membrane fluidity
Cholesterol only affects fluidity in plant cell membranes, not animal
bio.why: Cholesterol is a fluidity buffer. At low temperatures, it prevents tight crystalline packing of phospholipids (maintains some fluidity). At high temperatures, it restrains excessive lateral movement (prevents over-fluidization). The net effect: animal membranes maintain similar fluidity over a wider temperature range.

bio.q: Water can cross lipid bilayers slowly by simple diffusion, but in tissues with high water flux — kidney collecting ducts during ADH-induced water reabsorption, for example — the rate is dramatically increased by integral membrane proteins that form selective channels. What are these proteins called?
opts: Active transport pumps that use ATP to move water across the membrane
Aquaporins — selective channels that allow water (and some small uncharged molecules like glycerol) to flow through at high rates without permitting ion passage
Receptor kinases that signal membrane changes
Cell-surface glycoproteins involved in cell adhesion
bio.why: Aquaporins are integral membrane channels that allow water to cross the bilayer rapidly while excluding ions (their selectivity filter rejects charged species). In the kidney, ADH triggers insertion of AQP2 into collecting duct cells, dramatically increasing water reabsorption. The 2003 Nobel Prize in Chemistry honored aquaporin discovery.

bio.q: Protein kinases add phosphate groups to specific serine, threonine, or tyrosine residues, often turning a target enzyme on or off. The reverse reaction is catalyzed by a different family of enzymes that physiologically opposes kinase action. Which enzymes remove phosphate groups from proteins?
opts: Acetyltransferases (HATs), which transfer acetyl groups to lysines
Methyltransferases, which add methyl groups to histones
Protein phosphatases, which hydrolyze phosphoester bonds and remove phosphate groups (e.g., PP1, PP2A, PTP1B)
Glycosyltransferases, which add sugars to proteins
Sumoylation enzymes, which add SUMO to lysines
bio.why: Protein phosphatases reverse the action of kinases by hydrolyzing the phosphoester bond. They are equally critical to cellular signaling — kinase activation must be reversible to give the cell a switch rather than a stuck-on state. The major families are Ser/Thr phosphatases (PP1, PP2A, calcineurin) and tyrosine phosphatases (PTP1B, SHP2).

bio.q: Glycolysis produces a small amount of ATP directly via substrate-level phosphorylation, where a high-energy phosphorylated intermediate transfers its phosphate directly to ADP. Two specific glycolytic enzymes carry out this direct ATP-generating step. Which enzymes catalyze substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis?
opts: Hexokinase, which phosphorylates glucose using ATP (consumes, doesn't produce)
Phosphofructokinase-1, which converts fructose-6-P to fructose-1,6-bisP using ATP (consumes)
Phosphoglycerate kinase (PGK) and pyruvate kinase — both transfer phosphate from a high-energy intermediate to ADP, generating ATP
Aldolase, which splits fructose-1,6-bisP into two trioses (no ATP)
Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase, which produces NADH (not ATP)
bio.why: Substrate-level phosphorylation in glycolysis happens at two steps: PGK transfers phosphate from 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate to ADP, making ATP and 3-phosphoglycerate; pyruvate kinase transfers phosphate from phosphoenolpyruvate to ADP. Each step happens twice per glucose (once per triose), giving 4 ATP gross output, minus 2 ATP invested earlier = 2 ATP net.

bio.q: Pyruvate produced by glycolysis enters the mitochondrial matrix and is converted to acetyl-CoA by a large multienzyme complex (pyruvate dehydrogenase, PDH). This step links glycolysis to the citric acid cycle and is considered functionally irreversible. What does PDH catalyze?
opts: Pyruvate + CoA + NAD+ → acetyl-CoA + CO₂ + NADH (oxidative decarboxylation in the mitochondrial matrix)
Acetyl-CoA → citrate (this is citrate synthase, a Krebs enzyme)
bio.why: PDH catalyzes oxidative decarboxylation: pyruvate is decarboxylated (loses CO₂), the remaining 2-carbon acetyl group is attached to CoA-SH, and NAD+ is reduced to NADH. The reaction is exergonic and irreversible, locking pyruvate carbons into the Krebs cycle. PDH activity is heavily regulated by phosphorylation (PDK inactivates, PDP activates).

bio.q: The citric acid cycle generates ATP (or GTP) directly at one specific step via substrate-level phosphorylation. The high-energy thioester bond in succinyl-CoA is broken, and the released energy drives phosphorylation of GDP (or ADP). Which Krebs enzyme catalyzes this step?
opts: Citrate synthase, which condenses acetyl-CoA with oxaloacetate (no ATP made)
α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, which produces NADH and CO₂
Succinyl-CoA synthetase (succinyl-CoA → succinate + GTP/ATP), the substrate-level phosphorylation step of the cycle
Malate dehydrogenase, which oxidizes malate → oxaloacetate (NADH made, no ATP)
Isocitrate dehydrogenase, the rate-limiting step (NADH and CO₂ made, no ATP)
bio.why: Succinyl-CoA synthetase couples thioester hydrolysis (succinyl-CoA → succinate + CoA) with phosphorylation of GDP → GTP (or ADP → ATP, in some isoforms). This is the only substrate-level phosphorylation in the Krebs cycle. The other ATP from oxidation comes through the ETC after NADH/FADH₂ are reoxidized.

bio.q: After full aerobic catabolism of one glucose molecule (glycolysis + pyruvate decarboxylation + Krebs cycle), the bulk of the ATP is generated in mitochondria as NADH and FADH₂ feed electrons into the ETC, driving chemiosmosis through ATP synthase. Approximately how many ATP per glucose come from this oxidative phosphorylation alone?
opts: ~26-28 ATP from oxidative phosphorylation alone (out of ~30-32 total per glucose)
0 ATP, since oxidative phosphorylation does not generate ATP directly
bio.why: Per glucose, oxidative phosphorylation processes: 10 NADH (~2.5 ATP each = ~25) + 2 FADH₂ (~1.5 ATP each = 3) ≈ 26-28 ATP. Substrate-level phosphorylation contributes another ~4 (2 from glycolysis + 2 from Krebs). Total ~30-32 ATP per glucose, with the lion's share from oxidative phosphorylation.

bio.q: Intestinal epithelial cells absorb dietary glucose against its concentration gradient — moving glucose from low-concentration lumen into high-concentration cell interior. They achieve this without directly hydrolyzing ATP at the transporter; instead they exploit the steep Na+ gradient maintained elsewhere by Na+/K+-ATPase. What kind of transport is this?
opts: Primary active transport, since ATP is being used at the same membrane
Secondary active transport — SGLT couples 'downhill' Na+ entry with 'uphill' glucose entry, indirectly powered by the Na+ gradient that the Na+/K+-ATPase maintains
Facilitated diffusion through GLUT, no energy required
Simple diffusion across the lipid bilayer
Endocytosis, with glucose engulfed in vesicles
bio.why: SGLT (sodium-glucose cotransporter) uses secondary active transport. It moves glucose against its gradient by coupling movement to the favorable Na+ gradient — Na+ flows down its gradient and 'drags' glucose with it. The Na+ gradient itself is built by primary active transport (Na+/K+-ATPase using ATP) elsewhere on the cell. SGLT inhibitors are antidiabetic drugs (e.g., empagliflozin).

bio.q: The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) prevents anaphase from beginning until every chromosome is properly attached to spindle fibers from opposite poles. Until that condition is satisfied, the SAC inhibits a key cell-cycle E3 ubiquitin ligase that would otherwise trigger anaphase by ubiquitinating securin and cyclin B. Which complex does the SAC inhibit?
opts: Cyclin D-CDK4, which drives G1 progression
The anaphase-promoting complex/cyclosome (APC/C), the E3 ligase that, once active, ubiquitinates securin (releasing separase to cleave cohesin) and cyclin B (mitotic exit)
The retinoblastoma protein (Rb), which blocks G1/S progression
ATP synthase, the mitochondrial F0F1 enzyme
bio.why: The SAC inhibits APC/C^Cdc20 until all kinetochores are attached. Once attachment is complete, SAC release allows APC/C to ubiquitinate securin (whose destruction releases active separase, which cleaves cohesin) and cyclin B (mitotic exit). Loss of SAC function (e.g., Mad2 mutations) causes chromosomal instability, a hallmark of cancer.

bio.q: As a replication fork progresses through DNA, helicase unwinding generates positive supercoils ahead of the fork. Without intervention, the accumulating supercoils would block further unwinding. A specific class of enzyme makes transient cuts in DNA, allowing strands to relax, then reseals the cuts. Which enzyme is this?
opts: DNA ligase, which joins Okazaki fragments
DNA polymerase III, which synthesizes new DNA
Topoisomerase II (DNA gyrase in bacteria) — relieves supercoiling ahead of the replication fork by transiently cutting both strands, allowing relaxation, then resealing
Single-strand binding (SSB) protein, which stabilizes unwound DNA
bio.why: Topoisomerases relieve supercoiling. Type II (gyrase in bacteria, topo IV) cuts both DNA strands transiently, passes another duplex through, and reseals. Type I cuts one strand. Quinolone antibiotics (ciprofloxacin) inhibit bacterial gyrase, killing the cell. Topo II inhibitors (etoposide) are anticancer drugs that trap the cleaved intermediate.

bio.q: When a single mRNA is translated by many ribosomes simultaneously — each ribosome at a different stage along the mRNA — the structure looks like beads on a string under EM. This arrangement amplifies protein output per mRNA molecule and is especially prominent in tissues with high biosynthetic demand. What is this structure called?
opts: Polysome (polyribosome) — multiple ribosomes simultaneously translating one mRNA
Polyadenylated structures, with many adenines on one ribosome
Damaged or stalled ribosomes that cannot finish translation
Ribosomal storage particles for unused subunits
An RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) bound to the mRNA
bio.why: Polysomes are mRNAs simultaneously bound by multiple ribosomes (typically 1 ribosome per ~80 nt of mRNA). They greatly amplify protein output per mRNA. Active translation polysomes appear by EM as beads-on-a-string. Cells under stress disassemble polysomes (e.g., during the integrated stress response or amino acid deprivation).

bio.q: In Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Vmax represents the maximum rate of a reaction when the enzyme is fully saturated with substrate. Doubling the substrate concentration above this point cannot increase the rate. What primarily determines Vmax in a given experiment?
opts: Substrate concentration, since Vmax is reached at infinite [S]
Total enzyme concentration in the reaction, plus the enzyme's intrinsic kcat (turnover number); Vmax = kcat × [E]_total
Temperature only, with no enzyme dependence
Km (Michaelis constant), which is unrelated to Vmax
pH alone, regardless of enzyme amount
bio.why: Vmax = kcat × [E]_total. It depends on total enzyme concentration (more enzyme = more Vmax) and the enzyme's intrinsic turnover number (kcat). It does NOT depend on substrate concentration (as long as Vmax is approached). Increasing temperature can increase kcat to a point but eventually denatures the enzyme; pH affects kcat indirectly through residue protonation.

bio.q: The Lineweaver-Burk plot is a linearization of the Michaelis-Menten equation. It transforms the hyperbolic v vs [S] curve into a straight line, making it easier to estimate Vmax and Km from the intercepts. Which axes does the Lineweaver-Burk plot use?
opts: Velocity v on the y-axis vs substrate concentration [S] on the x-axis (the Michaelis-Menten plot itself)
1/v on the y-axis vs 1/[S] on the x-axis (the double-reciprocal plot); the y-intercept gives 1/Vmax and the x-intercept gives -1/Km
v vs log [S], which is the Hill plot
ΔG vs [S], showing the reaction energetics
bio.why: The Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot graphs 1/v vs 1/[S]. The Michaelis-Menten equation v = Vmax[S]/(Km + [S]) inverts to 1/v = (Km/Vmax)·(1/[S]) + 1/Vmax. y-intercept = 1/Vmax, x-intercept = -1/Km, slope = Km/Vmax. The double-reciprocal plot is the classic way to identify inhibitor types (competitive, non-competitive, uncompetitive).

bio.q: Lipase enzymes secreted by the pancreas hydrolyze triglycerides in the small intestine. The reaction cleaves the three ester bonds linking fatty-acid tails to the glycerol backbone, freeing the lipid components for absorption. What two product types are released?
opts: Glycerol (a 3-carbon trihydroxy alcohol) plus three fatty acids
Glucose plus fructose, the two sugar products of disaccharide hydrolysis
Amino acids (the products of protein hydrolysis)
bio.why: Lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides into one glycerol + three fatty acids. Bile salts emulsify fats first, increasing surface area for lipase action. The fatty acids and monoglycerides reform into mixed micelles, are absorbed into intestinal cells, reassembled into triglycerides, and packaged into chylomicrons for transport via the lymph.

bio.q: Fatty-acid catabolism oxidatively trims two-carbon acetyl-CoA units from the carboxyl end of an activated fatty acyl-CoA molecule. Each cycle generates one FADH₂, one NADH, and one acetyl-CoA. The pathway also requires functional mitochondria. Where does β-oxidation take place?
opts: Mitochondrial matrix (after fatty acids are imported via the carnitine shuttle), where β-oxidation enzymes reside
Endoplasmic reticulum, where fatty-acid synthesis occurs
Lysosome, the site of acid hydrolysis
Smooth ER, where lipid synthesis takes place
bio.why: β-oxidation occurs in the mitochondrial matrix (and to a smaller extent in peroxisomes, especially for very-long-chain fatty acids). Long-chain fatty acids must enter via the carnitine shuttle (carnitine palmitoyltransferase I/II), since CoA cannot cross the inner membrane. β-oxidation generates the acetyl-CoA that feeds the Krebs cycle, plus NADH/FADH₂ for the ETC.

bio.q: Cholesterol biosynthesis takes place primarily in the liver. The pathway condenses two-carbon units from acetyl-CoA in a series of reactions, eventually forming the four-fused-ring sterol skeleton through the key intermediate squalene. What is the starting material for cholesterol synthesis?
opts: Glucose, directly converted to the cholesterol ring
Acetyl-CoA — three molecules condense to form HMG-CoA, the precursor to mevalonate (the rate-limiting step) and ultimately squalene → cholesterol
bio.why: Cholesterol is built from acetyl-CoA. Three acetyl-CoA → HMG-CoA → mevalonate (catalyzed by HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting step). The mevalonate pathway eventually produces squalene, which cyclizes to lanosterol and then cholesterol. Statins inhibit HMG-CoA reductase to lower blood cholesterol — a $30B/year drug class.

bio.q: Skeletal muscle cells contain a specialized form of smooth endoplasmic reticulum that stores calcium ions at high concentration. When an action potential reaches the muscle fiber, calcium is rapidly released into the cytoplasm to trigger contraction. What is this specialized organelle called?
opts: Mitochondrial reticulum, used for ATP storage in muscle
Sarcoplasmic reticulum — the muscle-specific smooth ER, which stores Ca²⁺ and releases it through ryanodine receptors during excitation-contraction coupling
Cisternae, a generic term for ER stacks
T-tubules, which carry the action potential into the muscle fiber (a separate plasma-membrane structure)
bio.why: The sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) is a muscle-specific smooth ER that stores Ca²⁺ at ~1 mM (cytoplasmic resting [Ca²⁺] is ~100 nM). T-tubules invaginate from the plasma membrane to deliver action potentials deep into the fiber; voltage-sensors there trigger ryanodine receptors on the SR to release Ca²⁺, initiating contraction (excitation-contraction coupling).

bio.q: After S phase but before mitotic anaphase, each duplicated chromosome consists of two identical copies of the DNA, held together by cohesin most strongly at one specialized region. Each copy is referred to as a sister chromatid. How many sister chromatids does one chromosome contain after S phase but before anaphase?
opts: 1 chromatid (single, unreplicated chromosome — the G1 state)
2 sister chromatids, joined at the centromere by cohesin and identical in DNA sequence
Multiple chromatids (more than 2), one per gene
A random number of chromatids depending on cell type
0 chromatids — the chromosome is dissolved at this stage
bio.why: After S-phase replication, each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids — identical DNA copies — held together along their length and especially at the centromere by cohesin. The number of chromosomes is unchanged (e.g., 46 in humans), but each now has 2 chromatids = 92 DNA molecules. At anaphase, sisters separate to opposite poles.

bio.q: HIV is a retrovirus whose genome is a single-stranded RNA. After entering a host cell, the virus must convert its RNA genome into double-stranded DNA before it can integrate into the host genome and be transcribed by host machinery. Which viral enzyme catalyzes this RNA → DNA conversion?
opts: Host DNA polymerase, recruited from the nucleus
Reverse transcriptase, an RNA-dependent DNA polymerase that the retrovirus brings into the cell as part of its capsid
Host ribosomes, which translate RNA into DNA
An endonuclease that cuts host DNA at random sites
Integrase, which only handles integration of the proviral DNA
bio.why: Retroviruses (HIV, HTLV, etc.) carry reverse transcriptase as a virion protein. Once in the cell, RT copies the RNA genome to DNA (RNA-dependent DNA polymerase activity), then makes a complementary DNA strand to form double-stranded DNA, which is integrated by the viral integrase. RT's lack of proofreading is what makes HIV mutate so rapidly. Antiretrovirals (zidovudine, tenofovir) target RT.

bio.q: Tay-Sachs disease is caused by a homozygous loss-of-function mutation in HEXA, encoding the lysosomal enzyme β-hexosaminidase A. As a result, the lipid GM2-ganglioside accumulates in lysosomes (especially in neurons), causing developmental regression and early death. What general type of disorder does this represent?
opts: Lysosomal storage disease — missing a single hydrolase, so its substrate accumulates progressively in lysosomes, distending them and disrupting cell function
A disease caused by too many lysosomes per cell
A pH imbalance disorder, where lysosomes are no longer acidic
A membrane defect causing lysosomes to leak hydrolases into the cytoplasm
A metabolic disease unrelated to lysosomes
bio.why: Lysosomal storage diseases (Tay-Sachs, Gaucher, Fabry, Niemann-Pick, Hurler) are caused by single-hydrolase deficiencies. The undegraded substrate accumulates inside lysosomes, swelling them and disrupting cell function. Tissues with high turnover of the affected substrate (often neurons, given their lipid-rich membranes) are most affected. Treatments include enzyme replacement therapy and substrate reduction.

bio.q: A virus particle (virion) consists of a nucleic-acid genome (DNA or RNA) packaged inside a protein shell. The shell is built from many copies of a small number of distinct proteins, often arranged with helical or icosahedral symmetry. What is this protein shell composed of?
opts: A lipid bilayer with embedded proteins
Capsid — a shell built from many copies of capsomere proteins (a small number of distinct subunits arranged with regular geometric symmetry)
The viral nucleic acid itself, which doubles as the shell
Carbohydrate residues secreted by the host cell
An RNA-protein hybrid resembling a ribosome
bio.why: Viral capsids are built from capsomere proteins arranged with high symmetry (often helical, like tobacco mosaic virus, or icosahedral, like adenovirus). Some viruses also have a lipid envelope acquired from host membranes (e.g., HIV, influenza, SARS-CoV-2), but the capsid itself is protein.

bio.q: On a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot, a non-competitive inhibitor produces a characteristic graphical signature compared to the uninhibited reaction. Specifically, the y-intercept changes (since Vmax is reduced) but the x-intercept does not (since Km is unchanged). Which axis intercept changes for a non-competitive inhibitor?
opts: Same y-intercept, different x-intercept (this is the competitive pattern)
Different y-intercept, same x-intercept (non-competitive: 1/Vmax increases since Vmax decreased; 1/Km unchanged)
The slope is unchanged but both intercepts shift
bio.why: Non-competitive inhibitor: Vmax decreases (so 1/Vmax = y-intercept goes up), Km unchanged (so 1/Km = x-intercept unchanged). Lines intersect on the x-axis. Competitive: Vmax unchanged (same y-intercept), Km increases (different x-intercept). Uncompetitive: both Vmax and Km decrease (parallel lines).

bio.q: Sanger DNA sequencing — the dominant method until next-generation sequencing — uses chain-terminating nucleotide analogs that are incorporated into a growing DNA strand but lack the 3'-OH needed for further extension. The resulting fragments are separated by size to read the sequence. What are these terminator nucleotides called?
opts: Restriction enzymes, which cut at palindromic sequences
Dideoxynucleotides (ddNTPs) — they lack the 3'-OH, so DNA polymerase cannot extend the strand once incorporated, causing chain termination
Standard dNTPs, which always extend the chain normally
Reverse transcriptase substrates, used only in retroviral biology
Methylated nucleotides, which only modify base pairing
bio.why: Sanger sequencing uses ddNTPs (dideoxynucleotides). They are missing the 3'-OH, so once incorporated by DNA polymerase, no further nucleotide can be added — the chain terminates. Each ddNTP carries a different fluorescent label, and capillary electrophoresis separates fragments by size, reading the sequence base-by-base.

bio.q: A cell biologist wants to separate cellular organelles or molecular complexes that have similar mass but different densities. They layer the lysate on top of a tube containing a continuous gradient of sucrose (from low concentration at top to high at bottom) and centrifuge. Each component migrates to the layer matching its own density. Which centrifugation method is this?
opts: Differential centrifugation, which separates only by mass at fixed density
Sucrose-gradient (density-gradient) centrifugation, which separates particles by density (each migrates to its iso-density layer)
Microcentrifuge spin, used for small-volume sample concentration
Tabletop centrifuge, used for plate-format separations
Rate-zonal centrifugation, which separates by sedimentation rate
bio.why: Density-gradient (isopycnic) centrifugation uses a sucrose, CsCl, or Percoll gradient to separate particles by density. Each particle moves until it reaches the gradient point matching its own density and stops (zero net buoyant force). Differential centrifugation separates by mass (sequential pelleting at increasing speeds), which is a different principle.

bio.q: Many cell-surface proteins are decorated with covalently attached oligosaccharide chains, forming glycoproteins. These sugars project into the extracellular space, where they participate in cell-cell interactions, antigen recognition, and protection from proteases. What is the primary functional role of these glycoproteins on cell surfaces?
opts: Direct ATP synthesis at the plasma membrane
Cell-cell recognition (e.g., immune cell receptors, blood-group antigens) and signaling, plus protection of the protein backbone from proteolysis
Direct ion transport across the bilayer (which requires channels or pumps, not glycoproteins per se)
bio.why: Surface glycoproteins (and glycolipids) form the glycocalyx and serve as cell-cell recognition tags. ABO blood groups are oligosaccharides on RBC glycoproteins. Selectins on leukocytes recognize sugars on endothelial cells. The sugars also protect the protein backbone from proteases and contribute to the immune system's distinction of self from non-self.

bio.q: In Griffith's classic 1928 experiment, harmless R-strain pneumococci became virulent when mixed with heat-killed S-strain bacteria. Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty later showed that DNA was the transforming substance. The bacteria had taken up free DNA from their environment and integrated it into their genome. What is this form of horizontal gene transfer called?
opts: Transformation — uptake of free (naked) DNA from the environment, integrated into the recipient genome
Transduction, where DNA is delivered by a bacteriophage
Conjugation, which requires direct cell-to-cell contact via a sex pilus
Transposition, where mobile DNA jumps within a single genome
bio.why: Transformation is uptake of free DNA from the environment by 'competent' bacterial cells. Some species (e.g., Streptococcus, Bacillus) are naturally competent; others (e.g., E. coli) need artificial induction. Transformation was the basis of Avery-MacLeod-McCarty's identification of DNA as the genetic material in 1944.

bio.q: When a bacteriophage infects one bacterium and accidentally packages a piece of bacterial DNA inside a phage particle, that DNA can be delivered to a new bacterial host upon subsequent infection. The new host integrates the foreign DNA into its genome and acquires new traits. What is this mechanism called?
opts: Conjugation, mediated by a sex pilus

Transduction — DNA transferred between bacteria by a bacteriophage vector (generalized transduction packages random host DNA, specialized transduction packages specific genes flanking the prophage site)
Direct cell-cell contact like animal cell fusion
bio.why: Transduction is DNA transfer between bacteria via bacteriophage. Generalized transduction: phage accidentally packages random bacterial DNA. Specialized transduction: prophage excises imprecisely and carries adjacent host genes. Transduction is one of three major bacterial gene-transfer mechanisms (transformation, transduction, conjugation).

bio.q: Water (H₂O, MW 18) has a boiling point of 100 °C, while methane (CH₄, MW 16, similar size) boils at −161 °C. Even hydrogen sulfide (H₂S, MW 34, larger) boils at only −60 °C. Why does water have such an unusually high boiling point compared to molecules of similar size?
opts: Larger molecular mass — water is heavier than methane (only ~2 g/mol heavier; doesn't explain a 261 °C difference)
Extensive hydrogen bonding between water molecules (H attached to highly electronegative O), which requires significant energy to break before water can vaporize
Ionic bonds between water molecules, like in NaCl
Branched molecular structure that resists evaporation
Water is denser than other liquids of similar size
bio.why: Water's high boiling point reflects its extensive hydrogen-bond network. Each water molecule can form up to four H-bonds with neighbors. Vaporizing water requires breaking enough of these bonds to release individual molecules to the gas phase — far more energy than dispersing methane (no H-bonds) or H₂S (much weaker H-bonds; sulfur is less electronegative).

A researcher arrests a cell at the G2/M checkpoint by inhibiting the activity of CDK1 (Cdc2) using a small molecule. Which of the following events would most likely FAIL to occur after the arrest is reversed and the cell continues into M-phase?
opts: Lamin phosphorylation and nuclear envelope breakdown
Anaphase-promoting complex activation; cyclin B degradation
Sister chromatid alignment at the metaphase plate
bio.why: CDK1/cyclin B activity is required at multiple M-phase steps. APC activation and cyclin B degradation come AFTER metaphase via the SAC; even with restored CDK1, if APC is downstream, the failure mode would manifest there. The other events (lamin phosphorylation, SPB separation, H3 phosphorylation) are direct CDK1 substrates and proceed once CDK1 activity returns.

bio.q: A point mutation in a DNA-coding strand changes 5'-AAA-3' to 5'-AGA-3'. The original codon coded for lysine and the new codon codes for arginine. Which type of mutation is this and what is its likely functional consequence on a protein?
opts: Synonymous mutation; no change because both are basic
Missense mutation; conservative substitution (basic → basic), often functionally tolerated
Nonsense mutation; produces a stop codon early
Silent mutation in the wobble position
bio.why: AAA (Lys) → AGA (Arg) is a missense mutation but conservative — both are positively-charged residues. Side-chain physiochemistry is preserved, so functional consequence is often minimal compared to non-conservative changes (e.g., Lys → Glu).

bio.q: In a dihybrid cross involving two unlinked genes, parents AaBb × AaBb produce 800 offspring. Phenotype counts are: 460 A_B_, 152 A_bb, 158 aaB_, 30 aabb. What does the deviation from the expected 9:3:3:1 ratio suggest?
opts: The ratio matches 9:3:3:1; no deviation is meaningful
Linkage between the two genes; the 9:3:3:1 ratio is distorted because parental combinations are over-represented
Epistasis; the bb genotype is suppressed
Partial dominance; the AB combination shows incomplete penetrance
bio.why: Expected 9:3:3:1 of 800 = 450:150:150:50. Observed 460/152/158/30. The aabb class is 30 (vs expected 50) — significantly fewer. This suggests homozygous-recessive (aabb) is partially lethal, while other classes match expectations.

bio.q: A patient develops severe hypoxia at altitude. Their kidneys respond by increasing erythropoietin (EPO) secretion, which stimulates erythrocyte production. Over weeks, hemoglobin concentration rises and oxygen-carrying capacity increases. Which control system best characterizes this physiological response?
opts: Negative feedback loop with the bone marrow as the effector and red-cell mass as the controlled variable
Positive feedback loop maintained until oxygen normalizes
Direct neural reflex via the vagus nerve
bio.why: Hypoxia → EPO → erythrocyte production → increased oxygen delivery → restoration of oxygen sensing → reduced EPO. This is a classic negative-feedback homeostatic loop, with red-cell mass / oxygen carrying capacity as the controlled variable.

bio.q: A population of finches on an island shows two distinct beak-size morphs (small and large) but no intermediate-sized birds. Selection pressure favors both extremes due to two distinct food sources. Over generations, the intermediate phenotype becomes increasingly rare. This pattern is best classified as:
opts: Directional selection; one extreme is favored
Stabilizing selection; intermediate phenotypes are maintained
Disruptive (diversifying) selection; both extremes are favored, leading to potential speciation
Genetic drift; random loss of intermediate phenotypes
Bottleneck effect from a recent population crash
bio.why: When selection favors BOTH extremes against the intermediate, that's disruptive selection. It can lead to bimodal phenotype distributions and is one mechanism for sympatric speciation.

bio.q: In glycolysis, the conversion of fructose-1,6-bisphosphate to two trioses (DHAP and G3P) by aldolase is followed by triose phosphate isomerase converting DHAP to G3P. If a mutation in TPI eliminates its activity entirely, what is the IMMEDIATE biochemical consequence?
opts: DHAP accumulates; only one triose feeds into the lower glycolytic pathway, halving ATP yield per glucose
Glycolysis is unaffected; G3P comes only from the aldolase step
The pentose phosphate pathway compensates by re-routing G6P entirely
bio.why: TPI normally rescues DHAP by converting it into G3P, keeping the pathway funneling both trioses through. Without TPI, DHAP accumulates and only the aldolase-produced G3P proceeds to substrate-level phosphorylation, reducing ATP/glucose yield.

bio.q: A novel pathogen secretes a toxin that specifically inhibits eukaryotic elongation factor-2 (eEF-2) by ADP-ribosylation. Which of the following best describes the immediate cellular consequence in target cells?
opts: Cessation of cytoplasmic protein synthesis at the translocation step (ribosome stalls)
Block of mRNA capping and splicing
Disruption of the nuclear pore complex
bio.why: eEF-2 is required for ribosomal translocation during translation. ADP-ribosylation by toxins like diphtheria toxin renders eEF-2 inactive, halting cytoplasmic protein synthesis at the translocation step. Mitochondrial translation is unaffected.

bio.q: In a community with three trophic levels (producers, primary consumers, secondary consumers), the introduction of a top predator (a tertiary consumer) typically results in:
opts: Trophic cascade; secondary-consumer numbers decline, primary consumers rebound, producer biomass decreases
Trophic cascade; secondary-consumer numbers decline, primary consumers also decline, producer biomass INCREASES
No effect; the new predator only eats producers
Loss of primary consumers across the food web
bio.why: Adding a tertiary predator triggers a top-down trophic cascade: the new predator suppresses secondary consumers, which releases primary consumers from predation pressure (primary consumers rebound), and the increased primary-consumer grazing then reduces producer biomass. Option A describes this classic four-level cascade correctly.

ochem.q: Enantiopure (R)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane is dissolved in 80% aqueous ethanol at 50 degrees C and slowly converts to the corresponding alcohol. What stereochemical outcome at the original sp3 carbon is observed in the product mixture?
opts: Racemization producing roughly equal R and S alcohol
Loss of the stereocenter via elimination to an alkene
Formation of a meso diol after a second hydration
ochem.why: Tertiary substrates in polar protic solvent ionize to a planar sp2 carbocation in the rate-limiting step. Water can then attack from either face with similar probability, giving a near-racemic mixture and net loss of optical activity.

ochem.q: 1-Bromobutane is treated with NaCN in DMSO at 25 degrees C. The kinetics are first order in alkyl halide and first order in cyanide. Which description of the rate-limiting step is correct?
opts: Two-step ionization to a primary carbocation, then nucleophile capture
A single concerted bimolecular step with simultaneous bond making and breaking
Reversible carbocation formation followed by loss of a beta proton
Slow deprotonation alpha to the leaving group, then displacement
Pre-equilibrium solvolysis followed by SN1 capture by cyanide
ochem.why: Second-order kinetics (rate = k[RX][Nu]) signals a one-step concerted SN2 mechanism where the nucleophile attacks at the same time the leaving group departs. No carbocation intermediate forms, especially on primary carbons.

ochem.q: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is dissolved in methanol (acting as both solvent and nucleophile) and heated gently. Which mechanism best describes the dominant substitution pathway under these conditions?
opts: SN2, because methanol is a small nucleophile
SN1, because the tertiary carbocation is stabilized by the polar protic solvent
E2, because methanol acts as a strong base
Radical chain substitution initiated by trace peroxides
ochem.why: Tertiary substrates cannot undergo backside SN2 attack due to steric crowding. Polar protic solvents stabilize the carbocation and the leaving group, favoring ionization (SN1). Weak nucleophiles like methanol simply trap the cation after it forms.

ochem.q: Enantiopure (S)-2-bromobutane reacts with NaSH in acetone at room temperature to give the corresponding thiol. What stereochemical relationship does the product have to the starting material at the reactive carbon?
opts: Inversion of configuration via a Walden-type backside attack
Retention of configuration through a frontside displacement
Racemization through a planar carbocation intermediate
Complete loss of stereochemistry due to elimination
Net retention via a double-inversion neighboring-group pathway
ochem.why: SN2 on a secondary carbon with a strong nucleophile proceeds by backside attack 180 degrees from the leaving group. The three remaining substituents flip like an umbrella in the wind, giving inversion (Walden inversion) of configuration.

ochem.q: 2-Bromopentane is treated with potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butanol at 60 degrees C. Which mechanism dominates and what regiochemical outcome is expected for the alkene product?
opts: SN1 ionization followed by tert-butoxide capture
E1 with the more substituted Zaitsev alkene
E2 giving the less substituted (Hofmann) alkene due to the bulky base
Carbocation rearrangement to a tertiary cation, then E1
ochem.why: Bulky strong bases like t-BuOK cannot easily reach the more hindered internal beta-hydrogen, so they abstract the more accessible terminal beta-hydrogen. This concerted E2 pathway delivers the less substituted Hofmann alkene.

ochem.q: Enantiopure (R)-3-iodo-3-methylhexane is dissolved in 75% aqueous acetone and stirred at 40 degrees C. What is the expected stereochemical outcome at the carbon bearing the iodide in the alcohol product?
opts: Approximately 50/50 R and S product (racemic mixture)
No change because the C-I bond does not break
ochem.why: Tertiary substrates ionize in polar protic solvent to a planar carbocation. Solvent then attacks both faces with nearly equal probability, scrambling stereochemistry and producing a racemic SN1 alcohol mixture.

ochem.q: tert-Butyl chloride is heated in 80% aqueous ethanol with no added strong base or strong nucleophile. Which mechanism best accounts for the formation of tert-butyl alcohol under these conditions?
opts: SN1, via a tertiary carbocation stabilized by the protic solvent
SN2, with concerted backside attack by water
E2, with ethanol acting as a strong base
ochem.why: Tertiary halides in polar protic solvents lose the leaving group to form a stabilized 3 degrees carbocation in the rate-limiting step. The weak nucleophile (water/ethanol) then captures the cation, giving SN1 substitution.

ochem.q: 2-Iodo-2-methylpropane is stirred in pure methanol at 45 degrees C with no added base. Methyl tert-butyl ether forms slowly. Which mechanism best explains this transformation?
opts: Concerted SN2 backside attack by methanol
Stepwise SN1 ionization to a 3 degrees carbocation captured by methanol
E2 with methanol as a base, followed by re-addition
Carbene insertion of methylene into a C-O bond
ochem.why: Tertiary alkyl halides cannot undergo SN2 because of steric blocking of the backside. Polar protic methanol stabilizes the resulting tertiary carbocation; methanol then acts as a weak nucleophile to give SN1 product (the ether).

ochem.q: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is heated in pure ethanol at 70 degrees C with no added base. The product mixture contains alkenes and an ethyl ether in roughly comparable amounts. Which set of mechanisms best accounts for these products?
opts: E1 producing alkenes, alongside SN1 forming the ethyl ether
SN2 only, giving the ethyl ether exclusively
E2 only, giving Zaitsev alkene exclusively
SN1 only, giving the ethyl ether exclusively
ochem.why: Tertiary substrates in hot polar protic solvent generate a carbocation in the rate-limiting step. From there, loss of a beta-proton (E1) competes with capture by ethanol (SN1), so both elimination and substitution products form together.

ochem.q: Two elimination experiments on 2-bromobutane are run: one with concentrated NaOEt in ethanol, and one in aqueous acetone with no added base. Which mechanism's experimentally measured rate law contains the base concentration?
opts: Both E1 and E2 contain [base] in their rate laws
E1, because the carbocation must be deprotonated by base
E2, because the base removes a beta-proton in the rate-limiting step
Neither, because elimination is always solvent-driven
Only the SN2 competing pathway includes base
ochem.why: E2 is concerted and bimolecular, so the rate equals k[RX][base]. E1 has a slow ionization step that does not involve base; the base is consumed only after the rate-limiting step, so it does not appear in the rate law.

ochem.q: A student measures the rate of a beta-elimination of 2-chloro-2-methylpentane and finds rate = k[RX][NaOEt]. Which elimination mechanism is consistent with this rate expression?
ochem.why: A second-order rate law with both substrate and base implies a concerted, bimolecular transition state where C-H and C-X break while pi bond forms. That is the defining feature of E2.

ochem.q: Solvolysis of 2-chloro-2-methylpropane in 80% aqueous acetone follows the rate law rate = k[RX] with no [Nu] dependence. Which step is rate-limiting in this SN1 process?
opts: Ionization of the C-X bond to form a carbocation and free leaving group
Attack of water on the substrate before ionization
Loss of a beta-hydrogen from the cation
A single concerted step involving both substrate and nucleophile
Reversible protonation of the leaving group
ochem.why: An SN1 reaction's slow step is unimolecular C-X heterolysis, generating the carbocation. Because the nucleophile reacts only after this step, [Nu] does not appear in the rate law.

ochem.q: (S)-2-bromooctane reacts with NaN3 in DMSO. Doubling either the alkyl halide concentration or the azide concentration doubles the rate. Which step is rate-limiting?
opts: Two-step ionization to an octyl carbocation
A single concerted bimolecular step where Nu attacks as LG departs
Loss of a beta-H to give an alkene first
