Radical abstraction of bromine before substitution
ochem.why: When the rate depends on both [substrate] and [nucleophile], the mechanism is bimolecular and concerted. SN2 has a single transition state in which bond-making and bond-breaking happen simultaneously.

ochem.q: tert-Amyl bromide (2-bromo-2-methylbutane) is refluxed in ethanol for several hours with no added base. The product mixture contains 2-methyl-2-butene, 2-methyl-1-butene, and tert-amyl ethyl ether. Which mechanistic combination is responsible?
opts: SN2 only on a tertiary substrate
Pure E2 with ethanol as the base
ochem.why: Heating a tertiary alkyl halide in a polar protic solvent without strong base favors ionization. The resulting tertiary cation is partitioned between loss of a beta-H (E1, giving alkenes) and ethanol capture (SN1, giving ether).

ochem.q: A kinetic study of dehydrohalogenation of 2-bromobutane with NaOMe in MeOH reveals rate = k[2-bromobutane][NaOMe]. Which elimination mechanism includes base in its rate-determining step?
opts: Neither E1 nor E2 has base in the rate law
E1, because base attacks the carbocation
E2, because base removes the beta-H in the slow concerted step
Both have base in the rate law
Only E1cb mechanisms show this dependence
ochem.why: Bimolecular kinetics imply a concerted single-step transition state involving both substrate and base. That is E2: removal of the beta-H, formation of the pi bond, and loss of the leaving group all occur together.

ochem.q: Solvolysis of 1-bromo-1-methylcyclohexane in 70% aqueous acetone displays a rate law independent of nucleophile concentration. Which step is rate-determining for this SN1 pathway?
opts: Loss of an alpha-H to form a carbene
Heterolysis of the C-Br bond to form a tertiary carbocation
Initial protonation of the bromide leaving group
ochem.why: If [Nu] does not influence rate, then the nucleophile is not present in the slow step. Tertiary substrates ionize first to a stable 3 degrees carbocation; the nucleophile only traps it afterward.

ochem.q: 3-Iodo-3-ethylpentane (a fully tertiary alkyl iodide) is stirred in 90% aqueous methanol at 40 degrees C with no added base. Which substitution mechanism produces the observed methyl ether?
opts: E2 followed by re-addition of methanol
SN1 via a stable tertiary carbocation
SN2 by backside attack of methanol
ochem.why: Tertiary carbons block SN2 attack sterically. In a polar protic solvent, the C-I bond ionizes; the planar carbocation is then trapped by the weak nucleophile methanol, giving the SN1 ether.

ochem.q: 2-Chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane is dissolved in 80% aqueous ethanol at 50 degrees C with no added base. A small amount of rearranged product (3,3-dimethyl-2-butanol) is observed in addition to the tert-butyl-style alcohol. Which mechanism best explains the observation?
opts: SN1, because a 3 degrees cation can form and undergo a 1,2-hydride shift
E2 with the bulky internal proton
ochem.why: Carbocation rearrangements (hydride or methyl shifts) are diagnostic of SN1/E1 chemistry. Tertiary substrates in polar protic solvent ionize first; the resulting cation can shift to a more stable cation before the nucleophile attacks.

ochem.q: Optically active (R)-3-bromo-3-phenylhexane undergoes solvolysis in 80% aqueous acetone. The product 3-phenylhexan-3-ol shows essentially no optical rotation. What stereochemical outcome does this indicate at the original sp3 carbon?
opts: Net retention through a tight ion pair
No change because the C-Br bond does not break
Racemization through a planar benzylic carbocation
ochem.why: Loss of optical activity is a hallmark of SN1. The substrate ionizes to a flat sp2 cation (here, benzylic and tertiary), so the nucleophile attacks both faces with similar probability and yields a racemic alcohol.

ochem.q: When 2-bromopentane is treated with sodium ethoxide in ethanol, kinetic measurements give rate = k[2-bromopentane][NaOEt]. In which elimination mechanism does the base concentration appear in the rate law?
opts: E2, because base removes the beta-H in a concerted step
Only Hofmann elimination of ammonium salts
ochem.why: E2 requires the base to deprotonate the beta-carbon in the same step as C-X bond cleavage. That makes it bimolecular. E1's slow step is loss of the leaving group alone, so base does not enter the rate law.

ochem.q: An SN1 reaction of 2-bromo-2-methylbutane in 80% aqueous ethanol shows first-order kinetics in the substrate and zero-order dependence on water. A 1,2-hydride shift is observed in part of the product. Which step is rate-limiting?
opts: Attack of water on the carbocation
Heterolysis of the C-Br bond producing a tertiary carbocation
Loss of a beta-H from the alkyl halide
Methyl migration to form a more stable cation
ochem.why: First-order kinetics with no nucleophile dependence and observable rearrangement both diagnose carbocation formation as the slow step. After ionization, rearrangement and trapping by water occur in fast subsequent steps.

ochem.q: 1-Iodopentane reacts with 1.0 M NaCN in DMSO at 25 degrees C to produce hexanenitrile cleanly. Doubling either reactant doubles the rate. Which mechanism is operating, and why?
opts: SN2: primary substrate, strong nucleophile, polar aprotic solvent, second-order kinetics
SN1: a primary carbocation is uniquely stable in DMSO
E2: cyanide acts as a base on the beta-hydrogen
E1: ionization precedes loss of a proton
Radical chain substitution catalyzed by light
ochem.why: Primary alkyl halides don't form stable cations, so SN1/E1 are not viable. A strong nucleophile in a polar aprotic solvent (which de-shields the nucleophile) and bimolecular kinetics are textbook SN2 conditions.

ochem.q: (S)-2-Bromopentane is heated with potassium tert-butoxide in tert-butanol at 60 degrees C. The major product is the less substituted alkene 1-pentene rather than 2-pentene. Which mechanism is responsible?
opts: E2 favoring the Hofmann (less substituted) alkene because the bulky base targets the most accessible beta-H
E1 favoring the Zaitsev alkene through cation intermediacy
ochem.why: Bulky bases like t-BuOK can't fit at the more crowded internal beta-H, so they remove the more accessible terminal beta-H. The result is concerted bimolecular E2 that disobeys Zaitsev and gives the Hofmann alkene.

ochem.q: Solvolysis of 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane in 80% aqueous acetone follows rate = k[RX] with rearranged product detected. Which step controls the rate of this SN1 process?
opts: Backside attack of water on the alkyl halide
Heterolysis of the C-Cl bond producing the tertiary carbocation
Capture of the cation by water
Migration of a methyl group across the C-C bond
ochem.why: Independence of rate from nucleophile concentration, plus carbocation rearrangement, points to ionization as the slow step. Once the cation forms, rearrangement and trapping happen quickly in non-rate-determining steps.

ochem.q: 2-Iodopentane is treated with potassium tert-butoxide in t-BuOH at 65 degrees C. The major alkene is 1-pentene rather than 2-pentene. Which mechanism best explains this regiochemical outcome?
opts: E2 favoring the Hofmann (less substituted) product due to the bulky base
E1 favoring the Zaitsev product through a secondary carbocation
SN1 ionization with later proton loss to the more substituted face
ochem.why: Bulky strong bases force the elimination toward the less hindered beta-hydrogen, giving the less substituted Hofmann alkene. The reaction is concerted (E2) because the base is strong and the substrate is secondary.

ochem.q: Enantiopure (R)-2-iodobutane reacts with NaSCH3 in DMSO at 30 degrees C. The product is the corresponding sulfide with a measured optical rotation opposite in sign to the starting material. What stereochemical outcome at the reactive carbon explains this?
opts: Racemization through a flat carbocation intermediate
No change in configuration; the sign change is solvent-induced
Walden inversion via concerted backside SN2 attack
Retention of configuration via a frontside displacement
ochem.why: A strong nucleophile, a polar aprotic solvent, and a secondary substrate favor SN2. The nucleophile attacks 180 degrees from the leaving group, inverting all three remaining substituents (Walden inversion) and flipping the sign of rotation.

ochem.q: tert-Amyl chloride (2-chloro-2-methylbutane) is refluxed in ethanol for 12 hours with no added base. GC analysis shows mostly 2-methyl-2-butene plus minor 2-methyl-1-butene, along with some tert-amyl ethyl ether. Which mechanistic combination dominates?
opts: E2 only via ethanol as a strong base
E1 (giving the alkene mixture) with competing SN1 (giving the ether)
Pure SN1 with no alkene formation
ochem.why: Tertiary substrates in hot polar protic solvents ionize to a carbocation. From the cation, loss of a beta-H gives alkenes (E1, with Zaitsev preference) while solvent capture gives an ether (SN1). The product distribution is the classic E1/SN1 fingerprint.

ochem.q: Enantiopure (R)-2-bromooctane reacts with NaN3 (strong nucleophile) in dry DMF at 25 degrees C, giving (S)-2-azidooctane with high enantiomeric excess. What stereochemical outcome at the reactive carbon does this confirm?
opts: Racemization through a planar secondary carbocation
Retention of configuration via frontside attack
No change because the C-Br bond does not cleave
Walden inversion through concerted backside SN2
ochem.why: Polar aprotic DMF de-shields the nucleophile, accelerating SN2 attack on a secondary carbon. Backside attack of azide rotates the three remaining substituents 180 degrees, inverting absolute configuration (R becomes S).

ochem.q: (R)-3-Bromo-3-methylhexane is dissolved in 90% aqueous acetone at 35 degrees C. The alcohol product shows no measurable optical rotation despite starting from a single enantiomer. What stereochemical outcome explains the result?
opts: Loss of the stereocenter through alkene formation
Racemization through an achiral planar carbocation intermediate
ochem.why: Tertiary substrates ionize to a carbocation in polar protic solvent. The cation is flat (sp2), so water attacks both faces about equally, giving a 1:1 mixture of R and S alcohol that is optically inactive (racemic SN1 product).

ochem.q: (S)-2-iodooctane reacts with sodium iodide labeled with radioactive 131-I in dry acetone. The reaction follows second-order kinetics, and the product racemizes at twice the rate it incorporates 131-I. What stereochemical event explains the rate ratio?
opts: SN1 ionization with loss of stereochemistry
Each SN2 event with iodide inverts the carbon, so two displacements (one to S, one back to R) appear as one racemization event
Retention via a tight ion pair
ochem.why: Each backside SN2 attack by I- inverts configuration (Walden inversion). Two successive inversions return the molecule to the original configuration, so the molecule must invert twice to look 'racemized' once, giving the observed 2:1 ratio.

ochem.q: Consider (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane. Although it has two stereocenters, it possesses an internal mirror plane that relates one half of the molecule to the other. What classification best describes this molecule?
ochem.why: A molecule with chirality centers but an internal plane of symmetry is superimposable on its mirror image and is therefore achiral overall. This is the definition of a meso compound.

ochem.q: When assigning configuration at a stereocenter, the lowest-priority substituent is oriented toward the viewer (a 'wedge in') and the visible 1->2->3 priority arc traces clockwise. What is the true configuration?
opts: S, because viewing from the wrong side requires inverting the apparent direction
R, take the apparent rotation as drawn
Achiral; no configuration can be assigned
Meso, because the lowest priority is in front
ochem.why: CIP rules require viewing the stereocenter with the lowest-priority group pointing away. When it points toward you, the apparent rotation is reversed. Apparent clockwise therefore corresponds to true counterclockwise (S).

ochem.q: A compound has two stereocenters and is found to contain an internal mirror plane that interconverts the two halves. The molecule does not rotate plane-polarized light. Which classification fits?
opts: An enantiomer of an unrelated chiral isomer
ochem.why: Meso compounds contain stereocenters but also a symmetry element (typically a mirror plane) that makes them superimposable on their mirror images. The internal symmetry cancels their optical activity.

ochem.q: At a stereocenter, four substituents are -OH, -NH2, -CH3, and -H. Using Cahn-Ingold-Prelog rules based on atomic number at the first point of difference, what is the correct priority order from highest to lowest?
ochem.why: CIP priority at the first atom is by atomic number: O (8) > N (7) > C (6) > H (1). So -OH outranks -NH2, which outranks -CH3, which outranks -H.

ochem.q: Tartaric acid in its (2R,3S) form has two stereocenters connected by an internal mirror plane that exchanges them. What stereochemical category describes this isomer of tartaric acid?
opts: A meso compound (achiral despite chirality centers)
ochem.why: An internal mirror plane between two stereocenters relates the halves and makes the molecule superimposable on its mirror image. That is a meso compound; (2R,3S)-tartaric acid is the textbook example.

ochem.q: At a stereocenter, the lowest-priority substituent points away from the viewer. The 1->2->3 priority arc, viewed from the opposite side, sweeps clockwise. What is the configuration?
ochem.why: When the lowest-priority group is oriented away, the visible 1->2->3 rotation is read directly. Clockwise corresponds to R; counterclockwise would be S.

ochem.q: Consider (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane. Each carbon bears H, CH3, Br, and a different second carbon, so each is a CIP stereocenter. How many stereocenters does the molecule have?
ochem.why: Carbons 2 and 3 each carry four different substituents (H, CH3, Br, and a different remaining group), so they are independent stereocenters. The molecule has two even though it is meso.

ochem.q: (2R,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane is symmetric: each end of the molecule mirrors the other through a plane perpendicular to the C2-C3 bond. The compound is optically inactive in the pure state. Which classification fits?
opts: A racemic mixture of two enantiomers
A pair of enantiomers in dynamic equilibrium
ochem.why: Two stereocenters with an internal mirror plane create a molecule that is superimposable on its mirror image. Such molecules are meso and are intrinsically achiral, even as a single, pure compound.

ochem.q: How many CIP stereocenters are present in (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane, considering each carbon's substituents (H, CH3, Br, and the rest of the chain)?
ochem.why: Carbons 2 and 3 each have four distinct substituents and are stereocenters. The molecule has 2 stereocenters; despite being meso overall, each carbon still possesses stereogenic character.

ochem.q: While assigning a stereocenter on paper, a student notices that the lowest-priority group is drawn on a wedge coming out toward them. The visible 1->2->3 priority arc rotates clockwise. What is the actual configuration?
opts: S, because the apparent rotation must be flipped when the lowest priority points toward the viewer
Cannot be determined without a 3D model
ochem.why: CIP requires viewing with the lowest priority pointing away. When it points toward you, you see the 'wrong' side, so apparent clockwise rotation is really counterclockwise. The configuration is therefore S.

ochem.q: A drawing shows a stereocenter where the lowest-priority H points toward the viewer (a wedge) and the remaining 1->2->3 priorities trace clockwise. What is the actual CIP configuration?
opts: S, because the apparent direction must be inverted when lowest priority points toward you
R, taken directly from the drawing
Both R and S are possible
ochem.why: When the lowest priority is on a wedge (toward you), the apparent rotation must be reversed. A clockwise sweep as drawn corresponds to a true counterclockwise sweep, which is S.

ochem.q: (2R,3S)-Tartaric acid contains two stereocenters but possesses an internal mirror plane between C2 and C3. Pure samples do not rotate polarized light. Which stereochemical classification applies?
opts: A diastereomer of (2R,3S) without any symmetry
ochem.why: An internal mirror plane between the two stereocenters makes the molecule superimposable on its mirror image. It is achiral despite containing chirality centers, which is the definition of a meso compound.

ochem.q: A textbook drawing places the lowest-priority substituent on a wedge pointing toward the viewer at a stereocenter. The remaining priorities 1->2->3 are arranged clockwise. What is the actual configuration?
opts: S, since viewing from the front reverses the apparent direction
ochem.why: CIP requires viewing with the lowest-priority group away from the viewer. With it pointing toward the viewer, the rotation reads backward, so apparent clockwise (which would be R) is really S.

ochem.q: At a stereocenter, the lowest-priority substituent points directly away from the viewer (on a dashed bond). The visible 1->2->3 sweep is clockwise. What is the configuration?
ochem.why: With the lowest priority pointing away, the visible rotation is read directly. Clockwise corresponds to R (rectus). Counterclockwise would be S.

ochem.q: At a stereocenter the lowest-priority group lies on a dashed bond pointing into the page. The visible 1->2->3 priorities trace counterclockwise. What is the CIP configuration?
ochem.why: When the lowest priority is oriented away from the viewer, the visible rotation is the actual configuration. Counterclockwise (left-turning, sinister) corresponds to S.

ochem.q: (2R,3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane contains two stereocenters but is internally symmetric: a mirror plane runs perpendicular to the C2-C3 bond. The neat liquid has zero optical rotation. Which stereochemical descriptor fits?
ochem.why: An internal plane of symmetry makes the molecule superimposable on its mirror image; the optical rotations from each chiral half cancel. Such a single stereoisomer with no net chirality is a meso compound.

ochem.q: At a stereocenter the lowest-priority H is drawn on a dashed bond going into the page. The visible 1->2->3 priorities sweep clockwise around the carbon. What is the CIP configuration?
opts: Cannot be assigned without IR data
ochem.why: When the lowest-priority substituent points away, the visible rotation around the remaining three groups is read directly. A clockwise (rectus) sweep is R.

ochem.q: (2R,3S)-Tartaric acid contains two stereocenters yet does not rotate polarized light because an internal mirror plane bisects the molecule. Which stereochemical category applies?
ochem.why: Meso compounds have stereocenters but also possess an internal mirror plane (or other improper symmetry element) that makes the molecule superimposable on its mirror image. The two halves' rotations cancel.

ochem.q: A student examines a Fischer-style drawing where the lowest-priority H sits on a wedge pointing toward them. The 1->2->3 CIP priorities sweep clockwise. What is the actual configuration of the stereocenter?
opts: R, taken directly from the drawing
S, because viewing the wrong side flips the apparent rotation
ochem.why: When the lowest-priority group is on a wedge pointing toward you, the visible direction of rotation is opposite the true direction. Apparent clockwise therefore corresponds to true counterclockwise (S).

ochem.q: At a single stereocenter, the four substituents are -OH, -NH2, -CH3, and -H. Using Cahn-Ingold-Prelog rules and atomic number at the first point of difference, what is the priority order from highest to lowest?
ochem.why: First-atom priorities go by atomic number: O (8) > N (7) > C (6) > H (1). So -OH is highest, then -NH2, then -CH3, then -H. The order does not depend on what is further down the chain when the first atoms already differ.

ochem.q: (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane has each interior carbon bonded to H, CH3, Br, and a distinct remaining group. How many CIP stereocenters does this meso molecule formally contain?
ochem.why: Both C2 and C3 bear four different substituents (H, CH3, Br, and a different remainder of the chain), so each is a stereocenter. Two stereocenters can still be 'meso' if there is an internal mirror plane.

ochem.q: A compound contains exactly two stereocenters and an internal mirror plane that exchanges them. The pure compound is optically inactive at all wavelengths. Which stereochemical classification fits this description?
ochem.why: An internal mirror plane between two stereocenters generates a molecule that is superimposable on its mirror image. Such a molecule is achiral despite having chirality centers, which is the definition of a meso compound.

ochem.q: Cyclohexene is treated with O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degrees C, then a reductive workup with Zn in aqueous acetic acid. What is the expected major product after this two-step ozonolysis sequence?
ochem.why: Ozone cleaves the C=C bond to form an ozonide. Reductive workup (Zn/AcOH) yields aldehydes from each carbon of the original double bond. Cleaving cyclohexene's ring opens the chain into the dialdehyde hexanedial.

ochem.q: Propene is treated with dilute aqueous H2SO4 at 25 degrees C with no peroxides present. Following Markovnikov's rule, which alcohol forms as the major product?
ochem.why: Acid-catalyzed hydration adds H+ first to give the more stable carbocation; here, the secondary cation forms at C2. Water then adds at C2, and deprotonation gives 2-propanol. This is a textbook Markovnikov addition.

ochem.q: Propene is treated with 1 equivalent of Br2 in CCl4 at 0 degrees C in the dark. Which product, and with what stereochemistry where applicable, is expected?
opts: 1,2-Dibromopropane via anti addition through a bromonium ion intermediate
ochem.why: Br2 forms a cyclic bromonium ion across the double bond; bromide attacks the back face, giving anti addition. The product on propene is 1,2-dibromopropane. Light-free, halogenated solvents prevent radical allylic bromination.

ochem.q: Propene reacts with HBr in the presence of peroxides (e.g., ROOR) under radical conditions. Which alkyl bromide forms as the major product?
ochem.why: Peroxides switch the mechanism to a radical chain: Br radical adds first to the less substituted carbon to give the more stable secondary radical. H then caps the more substituted carbon, placing Br at C1. The result is anti-Markovnikov 1-bromopropane.

ochem.q: Propene is bubbled through anhydrous HBr at 0 degrees C in the absence of peroxides or light. What is the major product following Markovnikov's rule?
ochem.why: Without peroxides, ionic addition prevails. H+ adds first to give the more stable secondary carbocation at C2; Br- then attacks to give 2-bromopropane, the Markovnikov product.

ochem.q: Propene is treated with BH3 in THF at 0 degrees C, then oxidatively worked up with H2O2 and aqueous NaOH. What major alcohol forms, and what is its regiochemistry relative to the starting alkene?
opts: 1-Propanol; anti-Markovnikov, syn addition of H and OH
ochem.why: Hydroboration delivers BH3 with boron on the less hindered carbon (anti-Markovnikov) and adds H/B syn across the alkene. Oxidation with basic peroxide replaces B with OH with retention, giving anti-Markovnikov 1-propanol.

ochem.q: Propene is treated with cold, dilute, basic aqueous KMnO4. What is the major product of this oxidative addition?
ochem.why: Cold, dilute KMnO4 performs syn dihydroxylation across the double bond by way of a cyclic manganate ester. The two new OH groups are added on the same face. With propene, the product is 1,2-propanediol.

ochem.q: Propene is reacted with anhydrous HBr at 0 degrees C in the absence of peroxides. What is the major product of this ionic addition, and what regiochemical rule controls the outcome?
ochem.why: Ionic addition adds H+ first to form the more stable carbocation, and the secondary cation is favored over the primary one. Br- then traps the cation at C2, giving 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov product).

ochem.q: Propene is treated with cold dilute KMnO4 in basic aqueous solution. The reaction is kept ice-cold to avoid over-oxidation. What is the major product?
ochem.why: Cold, dilute KMnO4 in base performs syn dihydroxylation across the double bond via a cyclic manganate intermediate. Both OH groups add to the same face, giving 1,2-propanediol from propene.

ochem.q: Propene reacts with anhydrous HBr at 0 degrees C with no peroxides. Identify the major product and explain which regiochemistry rule applies.
opts: 2-Bromopropane (Markovnikov), through the more stable secondary carbocation
ochem.why: Ionic HBr addition proceeds through the more stable carbocation, which is secondary (at C2). Bromide adds to that cation to give 2-bromopropane. With no peroxides, the radical pathway is shut off and Markovnikov dominates.

ochem.q: Propene is treated with one equivalent of Br2 in CCl4 at 0 degrees C in the dark. What product and stereochemistry are expected from this electrophilic addition?
opts: 1,2-Dibromopropane via anti addition through a bromonium ion
ochem.why: Br2 forms a cyclic bromonium ion across the alkene. Bromide attacks the back face, opening the ring, so addition is anti (trans). On propene, this places Br on adjacent carbons to give 1,2-dibromopropane.

ochem.q: Propene is treated with BH3 in THF at 0 degrees C, then with H2O2 and aqueous NaOH. Predict the major product, including its regiochemistry relative to the original double bond.
opts: 1-Propanol; anti-Markovnikov, syn addition of H and OH
ochem.why: Hydroboration places boron on the less hindered (terminal) carbon with syn delivery of B and H. Oxidative workup converts B to OH with retention of configuration, giving anti-Markovnikov 1-propanol.

ochem.q: Propene is treated with dilute aqueous H2SO4 at 25 degrees C without peroxides. Which alcohol is the Markovnikov product, and what cation intermediate explains the regioselectivity?
opts: 2-Propanol via the more stable secondary carbocation
ochem.why: Acid-catalyzed hydration protonates the alkene to give the more stable carbocation; the secondary cation at C2 is favored over the primary at C1. Water traps it and deprotonation gives 2-propanol.

ochem.q: Propene is treated with cold, dilute, basic KMnO4 (the so-called Baeyer test conditions). What is the major product, and what stereochemistry does the addition follow?
ochem.why: Cold, dilute, basic KMnO4 forms a cyclic manganate ester across the alkene, then hydrolyzes to deliver two OH groups on the same face. The product on propene is 1,2-propanediol with syn stereochemistry.

ochem.q: Cyclohexene is treated with O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degrees C, then Zn/AcOH. What major product forms after this reductive ozonolysis?
ochem.why: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C bond. Reductive workup (Zn/AcOH) stops oxidation at the aldehyde stage. Cleaving the ring of cyclohexene opens it into the linear dialdehyde hexanedial.

ochem.q: Cyclohexene is treated with O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degrees C, followed by Zn/H2O. Which product results from this reductive ozonolysis?
ochem.why: Reductive workup of the ozonide preserves both new C=O bonds at the aldehyde oxidation level. Because cyclohexene's C=C is part of a ring, cleavage opens the ring into a single chain with aldehydes at each end (hexanedial).

ochem.q: Propene is hydrogenated with H2 (1 atm) over a Pd/C catalyst in ethanol at 25 degrees C. What is the product of this catalytic hydrogenation?
ochem.why: Pd/C with H2 performs syn addition of two H atoms across the C=C bond. With propene, both faces of the double bond accept hydrogen and the product is propane.

ochem.q: Propene reacts with HBr in the presence of dibenzoyl peroxide (a radical initiator). Which product is favored under these radical conditions?
ochem.why: Peroxides initiate a radical chain in which Br* adds first to the less substituted carbon to form the more stable secondary radical. H* then caps the more substituted carbon, giving anti-Markovnikov 1-bromopropane.

ochem.q: Propene is treated with cold, dilute KMnO4 in basic aqueous solution at 0 degrees C. Which product, with which stereochemistry, results from this Baeyer test?
opts: 1,2-Propanediol via syn dihydroxylation through a cyclic manganate ester
ochem.why: Cold, dilute KMnO4 forms a cyclic Mn(V) ester across the alkene. Hydrolysis gives a syn diol because both OH groups end up on the same face. With propene, the product is 1,2-propanediol.

ochem.q: Propene undergoes hydroboration with BH3 in THF at 0 degrees C, followed by basic peroxide workup (H2O2, NaOH). What is the major product, and what is the regio/stereochemistry of the overall transformation?
ochem.why: Hydroboration adds H and B across the alkene in a concerted, syn fashion with B on the less hindered carbon (anti-Markovnikov). Basic peroxide oxidation replaces C-B with C-OH stereospecifically, giving 1-propanol.

ochem.q: Cyclohexene is treated with O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degrees C, then with Zn/AcOH workup. Identify the major product and explain why a ring-opened compound forms instead of a cyclic ketone.
opts: Hexanedial; ozone cleaves the C=C bond, opening the ring into a chain with aldehydes at both ends
ochem.why: Ozone breaks the C=C bond and reductive workup gives carbonyls at the aldehyde stage. Because cyclohexene's double bond is part of the ring, cleaving it converts a cyclic alkene into an open dialdehyde chain (hexanedial).

ochem.q: Propene is treated with Br2 in CCl4 at 0 degrees C, kept in the dark to suppress radicals. What is the major product, and what stereochemistry does it inherit from the bromonium ion intermediate?
ochem.why: Br2 forms a bridged bromonium ion across the C=C; bromide opens it from the back face, so the two Br atoms add anti (trans). On propene this gives vicinal 1,2-dibromopropane.

ochem.q: Propene reacts with anhydrous HBr at 0 degrees C in the dark with no peroxides. Why does the Markovnikov product dominate, and what is it?
opts: 2-Bromopropane (Markovnikov); H+ adds to give the more stable secondary carbocation, which Br- traps
Propane; HBr is reduced to H2
ochem.why: Without peroxides, addition is ionic. Protonation gives the more stable carbocation, and a secondary cation is favored over a primary one. Bromide then captures the secondary cation to form 2-bromopropane.

ochem.q: Treating propene with one equivalent of Br2 in CCl4 at 0 degrees C in the dark gives anti addition. Identify the major product and explain the stereochemical outcome.
opts: 1,2-Dibromopropane formed via anti opening of a bridged bromonium ion
ochem.why: Br2 first forms a cyclic bromonium ion, then bromide attacks from the opposite face. The result is a vicinal dibromide with anti stereochemistry. On propene, this is 1,2-dibromopropane.

ochem.q: Propene is treated with dilute aqueous H2SO4 at 25 degrees C with no peroxides. Predict the major alcohol and explain why a primary product is not favored.
opts: 1-Propanol; primary cations are stabilized by hyperconjugation
Propanal via oxidation of the alkene
2-Propanol (Markovnikov); the secondary carbocation at C2 is more stable than the primary at C1
ochem.why: Acid-catalyzed hydration protonates the alkene to give the more stable carbocation. A secondary cation at C2 is much more stable than a primary cation at C1, so water adds at C2 to give 2-propanol.

ochem.q: Cyclohexene is exposed to O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degrees C and then worked up with Zn/AcOH (reductive conditions). Predict the major product and contrast it with what would form under oxidative workup.
opts: Cyclohexanone, since the ring is preserved
Hexanedioic acid (adipic acid), the oxidative-workup product
Hexanedial (open-chain dialdehyde) from reductive workup of the ozonide
Cyclohexanol from reduction of the alkene
ochem.why: Ozone cleaves the cyclic C=C and the ozonide is reduced by Zn/AcOH to two aldehydes, opening the ring into hexanedial. Oxidative workup (H2O2) would push the aldehydes to carboxylic acids (adipic acid).

ochem.q: Propene is treated with one equivalent of Br2 in CCl4 at 0 degrees C in the dark. What is the major product, and what mechanistic feature controls the stereochemistry?
opts: 1,2-Dibromopropane via anti opening of a bridged bromonium ion
ochem.why: Halogenation of an alkene proceeds through a cyclic halonium ion that is opened by the second halide on the opposite face. On propene, this generates the vicinal anti dibromide 1,2-dibromopropane.

ochem.q: Propene is treated with HBr in the presence of dibenzoyl peroxide at 80 degrees C. What is the major product, and which intermediate explains its anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry?
opts: 1-Bromopropane; the secondary radical formed by Br* addition to C1 is more stable than the primary one
ochem.why: With peroxides, HBr adds by a radical chain. Br* adds to the less substituted carbon (C1) to give the more stable secondary carbon radical at C2; H* then adds at C2. The Br ends up at C1, giving anti-Markovnikov 1-bromopropane.

ochem.q: 2-Butyne is hydrogenated with H2 over a Lindlar catalyst (Pd/CaCO3 poisoned with Pb, in quinoline). What is the major product and its geometry?
opts: cis-2-butene from syn addition stopped at the alkene
ochem.why: Lindlar's catalyst is a poisoned Pd that adds H2 only once and only on the same face. Both H atoms add syn to the same side of the alkyne, locking the alkene as cis (Z). 2-Butyne becomes cis-2-butene.

ochem.q: 1-Butyne is treated with NaNH2 in liquid NH3 at -33 degrees C. What is the major species formed, and which proton is removed?
opts: No reaction; sp3 C-H bonds are too weak to abstract
The acetylide anion via deprotonation of the terminal sp C-H (pKa ~25)
A carbanion at C4 via Sigma-bond metathesis
ochem.why: Terminal alkyne C-H bonds have pKa ~25, much more acidic than vinyl or allyl C-H bonds because the conjugate base sits in an sp orbital with high s character. NaNH2 (pKa of NH3 ~38) is strong enough to deprotonate to give the acetylide.

ochem.q: 1-Butyne reacts with NaNH2 in liquid ammonia. What product results from this acid-base reaction at the terminal carbon?
opts: No reaction because C-H bonds do not ionize
Vinyl anion from a CH=CH-CH3 fragment
ochem.why: Terminal alkynes are weak acids (pKa ~25) because the sp-hybridized C-H places the lone pair in a high-s-character orbital. NaNH2 (conjugate acid pKa ~38) removes the terminal H to give the acetylide nucleophile.

ochem.q: 1-Butyne is added to NaNH2 in liquid ammonia (-33 degrees C). What is the immediate organic product of this acid-base reaction?
opts: No reaction because alkynes are not acidic enough
ochem.why: Terminal alkynes have a relatively acidic sp C-H (pKa ~25). Sodium amide (pKa of conjugate acid ~38) is a strong enough base to deprotonate them, generating an sp-hybridized acetylide carbanion.

ochem.q: 1-Butyne is treated with NaNH2 in liquid NH3 at -33 degrees C. Which species forms after the acid-base step?
opts: A vinyl anion at the internal carbon
No reaction; bonds are too strong
ochem.why: Acetylene C-H bonds (pKa ~25) are more acidic than vinyl (pKa ~44) or alkyl (pKa ~50) bonds because the lone pair on the conjugate base resides in an sp orbital. Sodium amide easily abstracts that proton to give the acetylide.

ochem.q: 1-Butyne is added to a solution of NaNH2 in liquid NH3 to form a nucleophile that is later alkylated. What species does this acid-base step generate?
opts: A vinyl anion via deprotonation at sp2 carbon
The terminal acetylide anion via deprotonation at sp carbon
No reaction; pKa is too high
ochem.why: Acetylenic C-H bonds are unusually acidic (pKa ~25) because the sp orbital holding the lone pair has 50% s character, stabilizing the negative charge. NaNH2 readily removes that H to generate the acetylide nucleophile.

ochem.q: Treating 1-butyne with NaNH2 in liquid ammonia is a standard preparation for which intermediate used in alkylations and cuprate chemistry?
opts: A vinyl anion at the internal alkyne carbon
ochem.why: Terminal alkynes have an acidic sp C-H (pKa ~25). NaNH2 (pKa ~38) deprotonates it cleanly to give the sodium acetylide, a key nucleophile for SN2 alkylations and metal-mediated cross-couplings.

ochem.q: 2-Butyne is treated with sodium metal dissolved in liquid ammonia at -33 degrees C (a 'dissolving metal' reduction). What major product, and with what alkene geometry, is formed?
opts: trans-2-butene from anti addition through a vinyl radical/anion intermediate
ochem.why: Na/NH3 reduces alkynes by sequential single-electron transfers and protonations. The vinyl radical and anion adopt the more stable trans (E) geometry before the second protonation, locking in the trans alkene.

ochem.q: Acetylene (HC#CH) is treated with 2 equivalents of HBr in CH2Cl2 at 0 degC in the absence of peroxides. What is the major organic product after both additions are complete?
ochem.why: HBr adds to alkynes by Markovnikov regiochemistry in the absence of peroxides: the first equivalent gives vinyl bromide (CH2=CHBr). The second HBr addition is again Markovnikov because the Br on the alkene stabilizes the adjacent carbocation through lone-pair donation, so H goes to the CH2 end and Br adds to the carbon already bearing Br, giving the geminal dibromide CH3CHBr2.

ochem.q: 1-Butyne (CH3CH2C#CH) is treated with 1.0 equivalent of NaNH2 in liquid ammonia at -33 degC. Which species predominates after deprotonation is complete?
opts: The neutral starting alkyne (no acid-base reaction)
A carbanion at the propargylic CH2
ochem.why: The terminal alkyne C-H (pKa ~25) is by far the most acidic site because the resulting acetylide anion has its lone pair in an sp orbital with 50% s-character, holding charge close to the nucleus. NaNH2 (conjugate acid NH3, pKa ~38) is more than strong enough to deprotonate it cleanly, generating the 1-butynide acetylide.

ochem.q: 2-Butyne is hydrogenated using H2 over Lindlar's catalyst (Pd/CaCO3 poisoned with Pb and quinoline) in hexanes at room temperature. What is the geometry of the alkene product?
ochem.why: Lindlar's catalyst is a poisoned Pd surface that delivers both hydrogens to the same face of the alkyne (syn addition) and is deactivated enough to stop at the alkene stage. Syn addition across the internal alkyne places the two methyls on the same face, giving the (Z) (cis) alkene.

ochem.q: 1-Butyne is treated with dilute aqueous H2SO4 and a catalytic amount of HgSO4 at 60 degC. After tautomerization of the initially formed enol, what is the major isolated carbonyl product?
ochem.why: Hg(II)-catalyzed hydration of an alkyne is Markovnikov: water adds to the more substituted carbon (C2 of 1-butyne), giving the enol CH3CH2C(OH)=CH2. Keto-enol tautomerization always favors the carbonyl, so the enol shifts a proton to give the methyl ketone 2-butanone. Terminal alkynes always give methyl ketones under these conditions, never aldehydes.

ochem.q: 2-Butyne is reduced with sodium metal dissolved in liquid ammonia at -78 degC (dissolving-metal reduction). What is the stereochemistry of the alkene product?
ochem.why: Na/NH3 reduces alkynes via single-electron transfers that produce a trans-vinyl radical anion intermediate, where the two substituents minimize steric strain by sitting on opposite faces. Anti protonation locks in that geometry, so dissolving-metal reduction is the standard way to make (E) (trans) alkenes from internal alkynes.

ochem.q: 1-Butyne (pKa ~ 25) is treated with sodium amide (NaNH2, pKa of NH3 ~ 38) in dry THF at 0 degC. Which conjugate base is generated as the principal product?
opts: No deprotonation occurs (NaNH2 is too weak)
ochem.why: Comparing pKa values, NH3 (38) is far less acidic than the terminal alkyne C-H (25), so the equilibrium lies completely on the side of acetylide. The terminal C-H is acidic because the acetylide lone pair sits in an sp orbital (50% s-character), placing negative charge close to the nucleus and stabilizing the anion.

ochem.q: Treatment of 1-butyne with 1.1 equivalents of NaNH2 in NH3(l) at -33 degC removes the most acidic proton. Which carbanion is generated, and on which carbon does the negative charge reside?
opts: An allyl anion delocalized over C1-C2-C3
No reaction; alkyne C-H bonds are not acidic
A terminal acetylide anion at C1 (sp carbon)
An sp3 carbanion at the C3 propargylic position
ochem.why: Acidity tracks s-character of the orbital holding the lone pair: sp (terminal alkyne C-H, pKa ~25) >> sp2 (vinyl, ~44) > sp3 (alkyl/propargyl, ~50). The terminal C1-H is by far the most acidic site, so NaNH2 selectively removes it to give the C1 acetylide; the propargylic CH2 protons are far less acidic and are not touched.

ochem.q: 1-Butyne is subjected to acid-catalyzed hydration using H2O, dilute H2SO4, and a catalytic amount of HgSO4 at room temperature. Following Markovnikov addition and keto-enol tautomerization, what is the major product?
ochem.why: HgSO4/H2SO4 hydration of a terminal alkyne adds water in Markovnikov fashion, placing the OH on the internal (more substituted) carbon to give an enol. The enol then tautomerizes to the more stable keto form, and because OH ended up on C2, the carbonyl forms at C2, giving the methyl ketone 2-butanone.

ochem.q: 1-Butyne is hydrated with dilute H2SO4 and HgSO4 in aqueous THF. The initially formed Markovnikov enol tautomerizes under the acidic conditions. Which carbonyl compound is isolated as the dominant product, and why is it favored over its tautomer?
opts: 2-butanone, because the more substituted enol gives the thermodynamically stable methyl ketone
2-butanol, from net Markovnikov hydration without oxidation
Butanal, from anti-Markovnikov hydration via hydroboration
But-2-en-2-ol, the kinetic enol that fails to tautomerize
ochem.why: Markovnikov addition of water to 1-butyne puts OH on C2 (the more substituted alkyne carbon) to give but-1-en-2-ol. Keto-enol equilibrium overwhelmingly favors the carbonyl because the C=O bond is much stronger than C=C plus O-H, so the enol tautomerizes to give the methyl ketone, 2-butanone.

ochem.q: 2-Butyne is reduced using Na metal in liquid NH3 at -78 degC, proceeding through a trans-vinyl radical anion intermediate that protonates with anti geometry. What is the configuration of the resulting alkene?
opts: (E)-2-butene (trans), because the trans-vinyl anion is the stable intermediate
A 1:1 mixture of E and Z isomers
ochem.why: Dissolving-metal reduction (Na/NH3) generates a vinyl radical and then a vinyl anion intermediate; this anion adopts the trans configuration to minimize steric repulsion between the two substituents. Anti protonation preserves that geometry, giving the (E)-alkene as the only major product. This is the complementary partner to Lindlar's catalyst (which gives Z).

ochem.q: Benzene is treated with concentrated HNO3 in concentrated H2SO4 at 50 degC. The H2SO4 protonates HNO3 to generate the active electrophile NO2+. What is the major product of this electrophilic aromatic substitution?
ochem.why: In nitration, H2SO4 protonates HNO3 and dehydrates it to nitronium ion (NO2+), the actual electrophile. Benzene's pi system attacks NO2+ to form a sigma-complex (Wheland intermediate), and loss of H+ restores aromaticity, giving nitrobenzene. The strong driving force to regain aromatic stabilization is why EAS substitutes rather than adds.

ochem.q: Benzene is treated with 1.0 equivalent of Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at room temperature. The Lewis acid activates Br2 toward attack by the aromatic pi system. What is the major monosubstituted product?
ochem.why: FeBr3 polarizes the Br-Br bond to generate a more electrophilic Br+ equivalent (Br-FeBr3 complex). Benzene attacks to form a sigma complex; loss of H+ rearomatizes the ring to give bromobenzene. Aromatic stability prevents addition products like dibromocyclohexane, and a single equivalent of Br2 stops at monosubstitution since bromine itself is deactivating.

ochem.q: Benzene reacts with Br2 in the presence of a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 25 degC. Aromaticity is restored after loss of H+ from the Wheland (sigma) complex. What single product predominates?
ochem.why: EAS with Br2/FeBr3 follows the standard pathway: electrophilic attack by Br+, formation of a Wheland intermediate, and loss of H+ to restore aromaticity. The driving force is recovery of ~36 kcal/mol of aromatic stabilization, which is why substitution wins over addition. The result is bromobenzene; without light or peroxides, no radical side-chain bromination occurs.

ochem.q: On a benzene ring already bearing -Cl, -Br, or -F, a halogen substituent has unusual electronic behavior in electrophilic aromatic substitution. Which combination of activating/deactivating effect and directing effect best describes a halogen substituent?
opts: Deactivating but ortho/para directing (sigma withdrawal vs. pi donation)
Neither activating nor deactivating; ipso directing only
ochem.why: Halogens are the textbook exception: they withdraw electron density inductively through the sigma bond (electronegativity), which slows EAS overall (deactivating). However, they can donate a lone pair into the ring through resonance, and that pi donation specifically stabilizes the sigma-complex from ortho/para attack, making them ortho/para directors despite being deactivators.

ochem.q: Benzene is stirred with Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 in CCl4 at room temperature. After workup, what is the major product of the electrophilic aromatic substitution?
ochem.why: FeBr3 acts as a Lewis acid catalyst that polarizes Br2 into a more electrophilic species (effectively Br+). Benzene's pi cloud attacks, forming a Wheland intermediate, and proton loss rearomatizes the ring to give bromobenzene. With only 1 equivalent of Br2 and bromine being weakly deactivating, the reaction stops at monosubstitution.

ochem.q: Friedel-Crafts alkylation requires a relatively electron-rich aromatic ring to attack the carbocation electrophile. Which substrate fails to undergo Friedel-Crafts alkylation under standard AlCl3/RX conditions?
opts: Strongly deactivated rings such as nitrobenzene
ochem.why: Friedel-Crafts alkylation needs a sufficiently nucleophilic aromatic ring to attack the alkyl cation electrophile. Strong electron-withdrawing groups (-NO2, -CN, -SO3H, -COR) deplete pi density to the point that the ring cannot attack, and the carbocation electrophile reverts or polymerizes instead. Nitrobenzene is the classic 'won't-react' substrate for FC alkylation.

ochem.q: Nitrobenzene is treated with Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 80 degC. The -NO2 group is strongly deactivating and a meta director. What is the major monobromination product?
opts: No reaction occurs at any temperature
ochem.why: Drawing the resonance forms of the sigma complex shows that ortho and para attack place positive charge directly on the carbon bearing -NO2, which is severely destabilized by the electron-poor nitrogen. Meta attack avoids that conflict, so meta is the least bad option for a strong deactivator. Heat is required because the ring is deactivated, but meta is still the major regiochemistry, giving m-bromonitrobenzene.

ochem.q: Benzene is nitrated with a 1:1 mixture of concentrated HNO3 and concentrated H2SO4 at 50 degC. The active electrophile generated in situ is the nitronium ion (NO2+). What is the major aromatic product?
ochem.why: H2SO4 protonates HNO3 and dehydrates it to NO2+, the nitronium ion electrophile. Benzene attacks NO2+, forms a Wheland intermediate, and loses H+ to rearomatize, giving nitrobenzene. The aromatic ring is preserved (so no nitrocyclohexane), and the nitro group strongly deactivates the ring against further nitration under these conditions.

ochem.q: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, ortho/para-directing activators stabilize the sigma-complex by donating electron density into the ring. Which set lists only activating ortho/para directors?
ochem.why: Activating ortho/para directors are groups that donate electrons into the ring through pi resonance (-OH, -NH2, -OR, -NHR via lone pair donation) or through hyperconjugation/induction (alkyl groups). They stabilize the positive Wheland intermediate from ortho/para attack. Halogens are an exception (deactivating but o/p-directing), while -NO2, -COOH, and -CN are deactivating meta directors.

ochem.q: Benzene is treated with 1.0 equivalent of Br2 in CH2Cl2 at room temperature with a catalytic amount of FeBr3 as the Lewis acid. Which product results from electrophilic aromatic substitution?
ochem.why: FeBr3 polarizes Br-Br to make Br+ more available; benzene's pi system attacks to form a sigma complex, which loses H+ to recover aromaticity. With only one equivalent of Br2 and bromine being a deactivator, monobromination dominates and gives bromobenzene. Polar (ionic) conditions in the dark suppress radical side-chain pathways.

ochem.q: When benzene is combined with Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 25 degC in the dark (to suppress radical chemistry), the reaction proceeds via a Wheland intermediate. What is the major product?
ochem.why: With FeBr3 as a Lewis acid in the dark, the polar EAS pathway dominates: Br+ adds to benzene to form a Wheland intermediate, then H+ departs to restore aromaticity, giving bromobenzene. Dark conditions exclude the radical pathway that would give benzyl bromide, and aromatic stabilization (~36 kcal/mol) ensures substitution rather than addition.

ochem.q: Benzene is treated with one equivalent of Br2 in the presence of a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 30 degC. Which product is consistent with electrophilic aromatic substitution under these polar conditions?
ochem.why: Br2 alone is too weakly electrophilic for benzene, but FeBr3 forms a Br-Br-FeBr3 complex with much greater Br+ character. Benzene attacks, the sigma complex loses H+, and aromaticity returns, giving bromobenzene. Polar/ionic conditions favor EAS over radical (no light/peroxides), and aromaticity prevents addition products like dibromocyclohexane.

ochem.q: Nitrobenzene is brominated with Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 100 degC. The -NO2 group withdraws electron density both inductively and through resonance. Where does bromination occur and what is the major product?
opts: No reaction; nitrobenzene is inert to EAS
ochem.why: Drawing the sigma-complex resonance structures for ortho or para attack on nitrobenzene puts a positive charge directly on the ring carbon bearing the strongly electron-withdrawing -NO2 group, which is severely destabilizing. Meta attack avoids that overlap, making meta the most stable (least bad) sigma complex. Heat overcomes the deactivation but the directing preference is maintained, giving m-bromonitrobenzene.

ochem.q: Nitrobenzene reacts sluggishly with Br2/FeBr3 at elevated temperature. The strongly electron-withdrawing nitro group destabilizes the sigma-complex when ortho or para attack occurs. Which is the major monobromination product?
opts: An equal mix of o- and p-isomers
ochem.why: All meta-directing groups are deactivating because they pull electrons out of the ring; for -NO2, the resonance structures of ortho and para attack place positive charge adjacent to the electron-poor nitrogen, which is highly unstable. Meta attack puts the positive charge only on carbons not attached to -NO2, so it is the least destabilized pathway and gives m-bromonitrobenzene.

ochem.q: Toluene is treated with 1.0 equivalent of Br2 in CCl4 with catalytic FeBr3 at room temperature (polar, ionic conditions). Where does the methyl substituent steer electrophilic bromination?
opts: Benzyl bromide via radical side-chain bromination
ochem.why: Alkyl groups are weak activators and ortho/para directors because they donate electron density via hyperconjugation/induction to stabilize the positive sigma-complex when attack occurs ortho or para. Sterics make the para isomer the largest fraction with the ortho a smaller share; meta is disfavored. FeBr3 (polar conditions) ensures EAS rather than radical side-chain bromination.

ochem.q: Friedel-Crafts alkylation uses an alkyl carbocation electrophile generated from RCl/AlCl3, which requires a sufficiently nucleophilic aromatic substrate. Which substrate is essentially unreactive under standard FC alkylation conditions?
opts: Strongly deactivated rings such as nitrobenzene
ochem.why: Friedel-Crafts alkylation requires the ring to be at least as nucleophilic as benzene. Strongly deactivating groups (-NO2, -CN, -SO3H, -COR) drain enough pi density that the ring cannot effectively attack the alkyl cation, and the cation rearranges or polymerizes instead. Halobenzenes are deactivated but still react; nitrobenzene is the canonical 'fails FC alkylation' substrate.

ochem.q: Benzene is treated with one equivalent of Br2 in the presence of a catalytic amount of FeBr3. The mechanism involves attack on Br-FeBr3, formation of a sigma complex, and loss of H+ to restore aromaticity. What is the major product?
ochem.why: The mechanism is the textbook EAS: FeBr3 polarizes Br2 into a stronger Br+ source, the arene attacks to form a sigma (Wheland) complex, and loss of H+ regenerates aromaticity. Recovery of aromatic stabilization (~36 kcal/mol) makes substitution greatly preferred over addition, so the product is the flat aromatic bromobenzene.

ochem.q: Benzene is treated with a 1:1 mixture of concentrated HNO3 and H2SO4 at 50 degC. Sulfuric acid protonates HNO3, which loses water to give NO2+. After electrophilic substitution and rearomatization, which product is isolated?
ochem.why: H2SO4 generates the nitronium ion (NO2+) by protonating and dehydrating HNO3. The arene attacks NO2+ to form the sigma complex, and proton loss restores aromaticity to give nitrobenzene. The newly installed -NO2 is strongly deactivating, so a second nitration would require much harsher conditions and would go meta.

ochem.q: Benzene is brominated with Br2 (1.0 equiv) and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 in CH2Cl2 at room temperature. Although Br2 alone reacts only sluggishly with arenes, FeBr3 polarizes Br-Br to generate a stronger electrophile. What is the principal product?
ochem.why: Lewis acid activation by FeBr3 makes Br2 electrophilic enough for benzene to attack. The standard EAS pathway (sigma complex formation, then H+ loss) gives bromobenzene. Without a leaving group on the ring, no SNAr is possible; without light or peroxides, no radical side-chain bromination occurs.

ochem.q: Benzene reacts with one equivalent of Br2 in the presence of FeBr3 to deliver Br+ to the aromatic ring. Loss of an aromatic H+ regenerates the catalyst and gives a flat, aromatic product. What is the major isolated species?
ochem.why: EAS substitutes (rather than adds) because the arene regains its ~36 kcal/mol aromatic stabilization upon proton loss. With only 1 equivalent of Br2, the reaction stops cleanly after one substitution, and the catalyst (FeBr3) is regenerated by deprotonation. The flat, aromatic product is bromobenzene.

ochem.q: Benzene is treated with concentrated HNO3 in concentrated H2SO4 at approximately 50 degC. Once the nitronium ion (NO2+) attacks the aromatic ring and the sigma-complex loses H+, what is the major product?
ochem.why: Standard mixed-acid nitration produces NO2+ from HNO3 and H2SO4, which acts as the EAS electrophile on benzene. The sigma complex loses H+ to rearomatize, yielding nitrobenzene. The strongly deactivating -NO2 group prevents over-nitration under these conditions, so dinitration requires forcing conditions.

ochem.q: Nitrobenzene is brominated with Br2/FeBr3 at 130 degC. Resonance structures of the sigma-complex show that ortho and para attack place positive charge on the ring carbon bearing the electron-poor -NO2 group, which is destabilizing. Which product dominates?
opts: No reaction (the ring is fully deactivated)
ochem.why: When the question explicitly walks you through the resonance argument, it's telling you why -NO2 is a meta director: ortho/para attack leads to a sigma-complex where positive charge sits on the carbon bearing -NO2 (destabilizing). Meta attack avoids that conflict, making it the least bad pathway. Heat overcomes the deactivation, but selectivity stays meta, giving m-bromonitrobenzene.

ochem.q: Toluene is brominated with 1.0 equivalent of Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 in CH2Cl2 at room temperature (no light, no peroxides). Which regiochemistry results from electrophilic aromatic substitution on the methyl-substituted ring?
opts: Benzyl bromide via radical side-chain bromination
ochem.why: The methyl group is a weak activator and ortho/para director: it donates electron density via hyperconjugation/induction, stabilizing the sigma-complex when the new group ends up ortho or para. Sterics give a larger para fraction than ortho. FeBr3 + dark conditions select EAS over radical side-chain (NBS or Br2/light), so the ring brominates rather than the methyl group.

ochem.q: Benzene is treated with one equivalent of Br2 and a catalytic amount of FeBr3 at 25 degC in CH2Cl2. The reaction proceeds through formation of a sigma-complex (Wheland intermediate) and loss of an aromatic H+. What is the major product?
ochem.why: FeBr3 activates Br2 toward electrophilic attack; benzene's pi cloud forms a sigma complex with Br+, then H+ departs to restore aromaticity. Substitution rather than addition is the outcome because the arene regains its aromatic stabilization. With only 1 equivalent and -Br being deactivating, monobromination dominates, giving bromobenzene.

ochem.q: Benzene undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution with concentrated HNO3 in concentrated H2SO4 at 50 degC. The H2SO4 functions as both Bronsted acid and dehydrating agent to generate the nitronium ion (NO2+). What is the major product?
ochem.why: Under mixed-acid conditions, H2SO4 protonates HNO3 and removes water to generate NO2+, the electrophile. Benzene attacks NO2+ to form the sigma-complex, which loses H+ to restore aromaticity, yielding nitrobenzene. The aromatic ring stays intact (preventing nitrocyclohexane), and there is no oxidation pathway here to give benzoic acid.

ochem.q: Halogens (-Cl, -Br, -F) on benzene exhibit competing electronic effects: strong sigma withdrawal versus weak pi donation from a lone pair. How does this combination manifest in electrophilic aromatic substitution?
ochem.why: The two effects act on different things: inductive sigma withdrawal slows the overall reaction (deactivating), but pi donation of a halogen lone pair specifically stabilizes the sigma complex of ortho/para attack through resonance, beating out meta attack. The net result is that halogens are deactivating but ortho/para directing, the only group class with this combination.

ochem.q: An unsymmetrical 2,2-disubstituted epoxide is treated with NaOMe in methanol at room temperature (basic conditions). Where does the methoxide nucleophile attack the epoxide carbons?
opts: The less-substituted (less hindered) carbon, via SN2
No reaction; epoxides are inert to alkoxides
Exclusively the oxygen, giving an O-methylated species
ochem.why: Under basic (no acid) conditions, the epoxide oxygen is not protonated and ring opening is governed by sterics in a clean SN2: the nucleophile attacks the less-substituted, less-hindered carbon from the back side. There is no carbocation character, so the more-substituted carbon (electronically more polarized in acid) is not preferred.

ochem.q: An unsymmetrical 2,2-disubstituted epoxide is opened with HBr in CH2Cl2 at 0 degC. The acid first protonates the epoxide oxygen, and bromide then attacks one of the ring carbons. Where does Br- end up?
opts: On the more-substituted carbon (acid-catalyzed, partial carbocation character)
On the oxygen, giving an alkyl hypobromite
ochem.why: Under acidic conditions, HBr protonates the epoxide oxygen first, weakening the C-O bonds. The more-substituted carbon develops partial carbocation character (tertiary > secondary > primary) and stretches its C-O bond more, which makes it the better electrophile despite being more hindered. Br- attacks there, giving Markovnikov-like regiochemistry, opposite to base-mediated opening.

ochem.q: 1-Propanol is treated with Jones reagent (CrO3 in dilute aqueous H2SO4 with acetone as cosolvent) at 0 degC, with excess oxidant. What is the major isolated product after workup?
ochem.why: Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4/H2O/acetone) is a wet, strongly oxidizing chromium reagent. The aqueous acid hydrates the initial aldehyde to a gem-diol, which is then re-oxidized to the carboxylic acid. Primary alcohols thus go all the way to the carboxylic acid (propanoic acid here); to stop at the aldehyde, you need an anhydrous reagent like PCC.

ochem.q: 1-Propanol is oxidized using excess Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4 in aqueous acetone) at room temperature for 1 hour. Aqueous strong-oxidant conditions over-oxidize primary alcohols past the aldehyde stage. What is the major product?
ochem.why: Jones reagent contains water, which hydrates the propanal intermediate to a gem-diol; CrO3 then re-oxidizes that gem-diol to the carboxylic acid. Because the over-oxidation step is fast under aqueous acid, the reaction does not stop at the aldehyde stage and goes all the way to propanoic acid.

ochem.q: 1-Propanol is stirred with excess Jones reagent (CrO3, H2SO4, aqueous acetone) at 0 degC. The water present hydrates any aldehyde intermediate to a gem-diol, which is then oxidized further. What is the major final product?
ochem.why: The stem walks through the mechanism: water hydrates propanal to a gem-diol, and the gem-diol's C-H is then oxidized again by CrO3 to give the carboxylic acid. This is why aqueous chromium oxidants (like Jones) take primary alcohols to carboxylic acids rather than stopping at aldehydes; PCC, by contrast, has no water and stops at the aldehyde.

ochem.q: An unsymmetrical 2,2-disubstituted epoxide is opened by NaOMe in dry methanol at 25 degC under basic conditions. Without acid to polarize the C-O bonds, the regiochemistry is governed by sterics. Which site does methoxide attack?
opts: The less-substituted (less hindered) carbon via SN2
The oxygen atom, generating an oxocarbenium ion
ochem.why: In neutral or basic epoxide opening, there is no protonation to generate carbocation character, so the reaction is a textbook SN2 on the less-hindered ring carbon. The methoxide approaches from the back side opposite the oxygen, displacing it as an alkoxide. Steric (not electronic) factors dominate.

ochem.q: Under basic conditions, sodium methoxide opens 2,2-dimethyloxirane (isobutylene oxide) in MeOH at room temperature. With no protonation of the epoxide oxygen, regiochemistry is dictated by steric accessibility. Where does MeO- attack?
opts: On the oxygen, giving an O-methylated zwitterion
ochem.why: Without acid catalysis, the epoxide oxygen is a relatively poor leaving group and the reaction is a normal SN2: the nucleophile attacks the less-hindered carbon. In 2,2-dimethyloxirane, that is the CH2 end, since the geminal-dimethyl carbon is too crowded for backside attack.

ochem.q: The Williamson ether synthesis couples an alkoxide with an alkyl halide via SN2. To minimize competing E2 elimination from a hindered substrate, which combination of starting materials is preferred?
ochem.why: The Williamson ether synthesis is an SN2 reaction, so the alkyl halide should be primary (or methyl) to allow clean backside attack with minimal steric blocking. Using a tertiary alkyl halide instead leads almost exclusively to E2 elimination because the alkoxide is also a strong base. Pairing a primary halide with the alkoxide gives the highest ether yield.

ochem.q: tert-Butanol is heated with concentrated H2SO4 at 80 degC. The protonated alcohol loses water to give a stable tertiary carbocation, which then undergoes E1 elimination. What is the major organic product?
ochem.why: With concentrated H2SO4 and heat, tertiary alcohols undergo E1 dehydration: protonation of OH gives water as the leaving group, ionization yields a stable tertiary carbocation, then a beta-proton is lost to give the alkene. From tert-butanol, the only alkene possible is isobutylene (2-methylpropene).

ochem.q: 1-Propanol is treated with Jones reagent (CrO3 in dilute H2SO4, aqueous acetone) at room temperature with the alcohol added dropwise. The aqueous acid hydrates the initially formed aldehyde, which is then re-oxidized. What is isolated?
ochem.why: Jones is an aqueous chromium oxidant: water hydrates the propanal intermediate to a gem-diol, and CrO3 re-oxidizes the C-H of the diol to give propanoic acid. This is the standard way to take a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid; an anhydrous reagent (PCC) would be needed to stop at the aldehyde.

ochem.q: tert-Butanol is heated to 100 degC in concentrated H2SO4. After protonation and loss of water, the tertiary carbocation eliminates a beta-proton via E1. What is the major product of this acid-catalyzed dehydration?
ochem.why: Acid-catalyzed dehydration of tertiary alcohols proceeds through an E1 mechanism: H2SO4 protonates the OH, water leaves to give a tertiary carbocation (which is stable), and a beta-proton is removed by the conjugate base. From the symmetric tert-butyl cation, only one alkene is possible: isobutylene (2-methylpropene).

ochem.q: When designing a Williamson ether synthesis to make a methyl alkyl ether, the alkyl halide should be the less hindered partner so that SN2 outcompetes E2. Which combination is best?
ochem.why: The Williamson ether synthesis is an SN2 reaction, so steric crowding kills it: tertiary halides give E2 elimination instead. The optimal pairing places the alkyl group on the halide side as primary (or methyl) and the bulkier group on the alkoxide. Aryl halides don't work either because SN2 doesn't proceed on sp2 aromatic carbon.

ochem.q: 1-Propanol is stirred with excess Jones reagent (CrO3, H2SO4, aqueous acetone) at room temperature for 1 hour. Because water is present, any propanal intermediate is hydrated and oxidized again. What is isolated?
ochem.why: The mechanism of over-oxidation: water hydrates propanal to its gem-diol form, and CrO3 then oxidizes the gem-diol's C-H to a second C=O, giving the carboxylic acid. So aqueous chromium oxidations (Jones, K2Cr2O7) take primary alcohols all the way to carboxylic acids; here, propanoic acid.

ochem.q: An unsymmetrical 2,2-disubstituted epoxide is opened with HBr in ether at 0 degC. The acid protonates the oxygen, lengthening the C-O bond at the more-substituted carbon to give partial carbocation character. Where does Br- attack?
ochem.why: Acid catalysis flips epoxide regiochemistry compared to basic conditions. After protonation, the more-substituted carbon develops more positive (carbocation-like) character because tertiary > secondary > primary carbocation stability, and its C-O bond stretches. Br- therefore attacks the more-substituted carbon despite the steric hindrance, giving Markovnikov-like addition.

ochem.q: The Williamson ether synthesis is a classic backside SN2 displacement of a halide by an alkoxide. To synthesize a target ether without significant elimination byproducts, which substrate-nucleophile pair is preferred?
ochem.why: SN2 requires backside attack on a relatively unhindered electrophilic carbon. A primary alkyl halide is ideal because there is little steric blocking and the alkoxide (a strong base) won't have time to abstract a beta-proton (E2). Tertiary halides give E2 instead, and vinyl/aryl halides don't undergo SN2 at all.

ochem.q: tert-Butanol is heated to 80 degC with concentrated H2SO4. After protonation of the hydroxyl, water leaves to give a tertiary carbocation that loses a beta-proton in an E1 step. What is the principal product?
ochem.why: Tertiary alcohols dehydrate easily under H2SO4 because the intermediate carbocation is well-stabilized. From tert-butanol, deprotonation of any of the equivalent CH3 beta-positions on the tert-butyl cation gives the same alkene: isobutylene (2-methylpropene). 1-butene cannot form because the carbon skeleton lacks a CH2-CH3 chain.

ochem.q: In a Williamson ether synthesis, the SN2 displacement of halide by alkoxide is the most common scheme. To avoid significant E2 elimination from the bulky alkoxide, which combination of partners is best?
opts: Tertiary alkyl halide + alcohol with H+
ochem.why: Alkoxides are strong bases as well as nucleophiles, so any time the alkyl halide is hindered (secondary or tertiary), E2 elimination dominates. Picking a primary halide and putting the bulkier piece on the alkoxide side ensures clean SN2 because the primary carbon is sterically open for backside attack.

ochem.q: A target ether is to be made by Williamson ether synthesis. SN2 backside attack on the alkyl halide by the alkoxide must outpace E2 elimination, so steric crowding on the electrophile must be minimized. Which combination is preferred?
ochem.why: The competition between SN2 (gives ether) and E2 (gives alkene) is decided by sterics on the electrophile: bulkier halides shift the balance toward elimination. A primary alkyl halide minimizes that crowding, letting SN2 win cleanly. Aryl halides cannot undergo SN2 because the sp2 carbon and ring geometry block backside attack.

ochem.q: 2-Propanol is treated with PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate) in CH2Cl2 at 25 degC, or alternatively with Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4) at 0 degC. A secondary alcohol cannot be over-oxidized because it lacks an alpha-hydrogen-bearing carbonyl carbon. What is the product?
ochem.why: Secondary alcohols give ketones on oxidation, and the reaction stops there because the resulting ketone has no C-H on the carbonyl carbon for further oxidation. Both PCC (anhydrous) and Jones reagent (aqueous) thus produce the same ketone from 2-propanol, namely acetone. Only primary alcohols differ between PCC (stops at aldehyde) and Jones (over-oxidizes to acid).

ochem.q: When planning a Williamson ether synthesis, choose the alkyl halide and alkoxide so that SN2 occurs cleanly on a sterically uncluttered carbon. Which combination is preferred when forming an unsymmetrical ether?
ochem.why: Always assign the alkyl halide to the less hindered partner because SN2 needs backside access to the electrophilic carbon. Primary halides allow clean substitution; tertiary halides give E2 elimination; and vinyl/aryl halides simply don't undergo SN2 because their sp2 carbons can't accept backside attack.

ochem.q: 2-Propanol is oxidized at 0 degC using either PCC in CH2Cl2 or Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4 in aqueous acetone). Because the substrate is a secondary alcohol, both reagents stop at the same oxidation state. What is the major product?
ochem.why: Secondary alcohols oxidize to ketones, and ketones cannot be further oxidized under these conditions because they lack an H on the carbonyl carbon. So the choice of PCC (anhydrous, stops at aldehyde for primary) vs. Jones (aqueous, goes to acid for primary) is irrelevant for a secondary alcohol; both give the same ketone, acetone.

ochem.q: tert-Butanol is heated to 90 degC in concentrated H2SO4 with no nucleophile present. The protonated alcohol loses water to form a tertiary carbocation, which loses a beta-proton in an E1 elimination. What is the principal organic product?
ochem.why: Hot concentrated H2SO4 dehydrates tertiary alcohols by E1: protonation of OH, loss of water to give a stable tertiary carbocation, then deprotonation of a beta-CH3 by the conjugate base. The tert-butyl cation has only one type of beta-H (all three CH3 groups are equivalent), so the only possible alkene is isobutylene (2-methylpropene).

ochem.q: A Williamson ether synthesis to form an unsymmetrical ether (R-O-R') requires the alkoxide to attack the alkyl halide via SN2. The alkyl halide should therefore have minimal steric hindrance to maximize ether yield over alkene formation. Which combination is preferred?
ochem.why: When making an unsymmetrical ether by Williamson, dissect it so that the alkyl halide carries the less hindered alkyl group (primary or methyl) and the alkoxide carries the bulkier group. Primary halides allow clean SN2 with minimal E2 competition, so this pairing maximizes ether yield. Aryl halides fail entirely because their sp2 carbon cannot undergo backside SN2.

ochem.q: An aldehyde is treated with 2 equivalents of ethanol and a catalytic amount of p-TsOH in dry benzene with a Dean-Stark trap to remove water. What functional group is present in the major product?
opts: Acetal (two OR groups on the same carbon)
ochem.why: Acid-catalyzed reaction of an aldehyde with 2 equivalents of alcohol gives an acetal: the first ROH adds to give a hemiacetal, the OH is then protonated and lost as water (driven by the Dean-Stark trap), and a second ROH adds to give R-CH(OR')2. Removing water with the Dean-Stark trap is the key shift that pushes the equilibrium past the hemiacetal to the acetal.

ochem.q: Two molecules of acetone are combined with a catalytic amount of dilute NaOH at 25 degC, then warmed to 60 degC. What sequence of products best describes this aldol process?
opts: Diacetone alcohol (beta-hydroxy ketone), which dehydrates on heating to mesityl oxide
ochem.why: NaOH deprotonates one acetone at the alpha-carbon to form an enolate, which attacks the carbonyl of a second acetone, giving the beta-hydroxy ketone diacetone alcohol (4-hydroxy-4-methyl-2-pentanone). On heating, E1cb dehydration loses the beta-OH (as water) to form the alpha,beta-unsaturated ketone mesityl oxide. This two-step aldol addition-then-condensation is the classic acetone aldol.

ochem.q: Propanal is stirred with 2 equivalents of ethanol and a catalytic amount of HCl in dry benzene with molecular sieves to absorb water. What is the functional class of the major isolated product?
opts: Acetal (two OR groups on the same carbon)
ochem.why: Under acid catalysis with 2 equivalents of alcohol and a water scavenger, an aldehyde forms an acetal: protonation, addition of ROH, loss of water (driven by the molecular sieves), and addition of a second ROH gives R-CH(OR')2. Without water removal, the equilibrium would favor the starting aldehyde plus alcohol over the acetal.

ochem.q: 2-Butanone is treated with 1.0 equivalent of LiAlH4 in dry THF at 0 degC, followed by aqueous workup. Hydride is delivered to the carbonyl carbon and the alkoxide is protonated. What functional group results?
ochem.why: LiAlH4 delivers hydride to the carbonyl carbon, and aqueous workup protonates the alkoxide. Reduction of a ketone gives a secondary alcohol because the resulting carbon bears one H (from hydride) and two carbon substituents (from the original ketone); aldehydes give primary alcohols; esters give primary alcohols; only addition of two carbon nucleophiles to an ester would give a tertiary alcohol.

ochem.q: Propanal is treated with 1.1 equivalents of ethylmagnesium bromide (EtMgBr) in dry diethyl ether at 0 degC, followed by aqueous NH4Cl workup. The carbanion adds once to the carbonyl carbon. What functional group results?
ochem.why: Grignard addition to an aldehyde gives a secondary alcohol: the carbon that was C=O now bears one H (from the original aldehyde), one R (the new ethyl from the Grignard), and one R' (the original chain). Aldehyde + Grignard always gives a secondary alcohol; ketones give tertiary; formaldehyde is the only carbonyl that gives a primary.

ochem.q: Two molecules of acetone are mixed with a catalytic amount of NaOH in water at 30 degC and the mixture is warmed to drive off water. Which product set best describes this base-catalyzed aldol condensation?
opts: Diacetone alcohol (beta-hydroxy ketone), dehydrating to mesityl oxide on heating
ochem.why: Catalytic base creates an acetone enolate that attacks a second acetone carbonyl, forming the beta-hydroxy ketone diacetone alcohol. Heat then drives E1cb elimination of water to give the alpha,beta-unsaturated enone mesityl oxide. This is the classic acetone aldol-then-condensation sequence (addition first, dehydration on heating).

ochem.q: 2-Butanone is treated with 1.1 equivalents of methylmagnesium bromide (MeMgBr) in dry THF at 0 degC, followed by aqueous workup. Methyl carbanion adds to the carbonyl carbon, generating an alkoxide that is protonated. What functional group results?
ochem.why: Grignard addition to a ketone gives a tertiary alcohol because the original carbonyl carbon already bore two R groups, and the Grignard adds a third. So 2-butanone (CH3COCH2CH3) plus MeMgBr puts a new methyl on the carbonyl carbon, giving 2-methyl-2-butanol, a tertiary alcohol.

ochem.q: Butanal is treated with 1.1 equivalents of CH3MgBr in dry diethyl ether at 0 degC, then quenched with saturated aqueous NH4Cl. What functional group is present in the major product?
ochem.why: Grignard addition to an aldehyde always gives a secondary alcohol: the former carbonyl carbon ends up with one H (from the aldehyde), the new alkyl group (from the Grignard), and the rest of the parent chain. Butanal + MeMgBr therefore gives 2-pentanol, a secondary alcohol.

ochem.q: Acetaldehyde is treated with 1.0 equivalent of phenylmagnesium bromide (PhMgBr) in dry THF at 0 degC, followed by aqueous NH4Cl workup. The Grignard delivers a phenyl carbanion to the carbonyl carbon. What functional group results?
ochem.why: Phenyl carbanion (from PhMgBr) is just another carbon nucleophile, so the rule still applies: aldehyde + Grignard gives a secondary alcohol. Acetaldehyde (CH3CHO) plus PhMgBr installs a phenyl on the carbonyl carbon, giving 1-phenylethanol (a secondary alcohol with H, methyl, and phenyl on the new sp3 carbon).

ochem.q: An aldehyde is heated with 2 equivalents of ethanol and a catalytic amount of p-TsOH in dry toluene, with water removed by a Dean-Stark trap to drive the equilibrium forward. What is the functional class of the major product?
ochem.why: The acetal-formation equilibrium (aldehyde + 2 ROH = acetal + H2O) is normally unfavorable, but a Dean-Stark trap continuously removes water, pushing the equilibrium toward the acetal by Le Chatelier's principle. Two ethoxy groups end up on the original carbonyl carbon, giving R-CH(OEt)2.

ochem.q: Benzaldehyde is treated with 1.1 equivalents of methylmagnesium bromide in dry THF at 0 degC, then quenched with aqueous NH4Cl. Methyl carbanion adds to the C=O of an aldehyde. What functional group is present in the product?
ochem.why: Grignard addition to an aldehyde gives a secondary alcohol because the new sp3 carbon bears H (from the aldehyde), a new alkyl group (from the Grignard), and the rest of the parent (here, phenyl). Benzaldehyde plus MeMgBr gives 1-phenylethanol, a secondary alcohol.

ochem.q: Two molecules of acetone are combined with a catalytic amount of dilute NaOH in water and warmed gently. After the initial aldol addition, the mixture is heated to drive off water. Which sequence describes the products?
opts: Diacetone alcohol (beta-hydroxy ketone), which dehydrates to mesityl oxide on heating
ochem.why: Aldol addition: NaOH deprotonates one acetone alpha-CH to give an enolate, which attacks a second acetone's carbonyl, giving diacetone alcohol (a beta-hydroxy ketone). On heating, E1cb dehydration eliminates water to give the conjugated enone mesityl oxide. Claisen condensation requires esters (not ketones) and would give a beta-ketoester, not a beta-hydroxy ketone.

ochem.q: Cyclohexanone is treated with 1.0 equivalent of LiAlH4 in dry THF at 0 degC, followed by careful aqueous workup. Hydride is delivered to the carbonyl carbon, generating an alkoxide that is protonated on workup. What is the product?
