ochem.why: Strongest base = weakest conjugate acid. Conjugate-acid pKa values: acetic acid ~5, methanol ~16, acetylene ~25, ethane ~50. The largest pKa belongs to ethane, so its conjugate base (ethanide) is by far the strongest base.

ochem.q: Boron trifluoride reacts with ammonia in the gas phase to form the adduct F3B-NH3. Identify the Lewis acid and the Lewis base, and explain the bonding.
opts: BF3 is the Lewis acid (empty p orbital on boron accepts the lone pair); NH3 is the Lewis base donor
NH3 is the Lewis acid; BF3 is the Lewis base
Both are Lewis acids; no bond forms
Both are Lewis bases; product is ionic
Neither — this is a Brønsted equilibrium
ochem.why: Lewis acid = electron-pair acceptor; Lewis base = electron-pair donor. BF3 has only six valence electrons on boron and an empty p orbital; NH3 has a lone pair on N. Donation from N into B forms a dative bond.

ochem.q: An IR spectrum shows a very broad O-H stretch from ~2500-3300 cm-1 superimposed on a sharp C=O stretch near 1710 cm-1. Which functional group best matches both features simultaneously?
ochem.why: Carboxylic acids show an extremely broad, dimer-H-bonded O-H stretch from ~2500-3300 cm-1 that often blankets the C-H region, plus a strong C=O near 1710 cm-1. Alcohols lack the C=O; amides show N-H instead of broad O-H.

ochem.q: An IR spectrum of an unknown shows a sharp, medium-intensity peak at 2210 cm-1 with no broad features and no peak near 1700 cm-1. The functional group most consistent with this absorption is:
ochem.why: Triple bonds absorb in the 2100-2260 cm-1 region. Nitriles (C≡N) appear sharp around 2200-2260, while terminal alkynes (C≡C) are weaker and slightly lower (~2100-2150). The 2210 cm-1 peak fits a nitrile.

ochem.q: A 1H NMR shows a triplet at 1.2 ppm (3H) coupled (J ~7 Hz) to a quartet at 3.7 ppm (2H), with no other multiplets nearby. The chemical shift of the quartet suggests an oxygen-bearing CH2. Which fragment is consistent?
ochem.why: Triplet/quartet (3H/2H) is the n+1 signature of an isolated -CH2-CH3 ethyl group. The OCH2 sits at 3.7 ppm because oxygen deshields it; the CH3 at 1.2 ppm is unaffected. Together they define an ethoxy (-OCH2CH3) fragment.

ochem.q: A 13C NMR spectrum has a peak at 205 ppm with no peaks between 165-180 ppm. Which functional group accounts for the 205 ppm signal?
ochem.why: Aldehyde and ketone carbonyls appear furthest downfield in 13C, around 190-210 ppm. Esters, amides, and acids fall around 165-180 ppm because the heteroatom donates electron density to the carbonyl carbon, reducing deshielding.

ochem.q: Compute the degrees of unsaturation (index of hydrogen deficiency) for the molecular formula C5H10. Use the formula DoU = (2C + 2 + N - H - X)/2.
opts: 2 (two rings, two pi bonds, or one triple bond)
ochem.why: DoU = (2(5) + 2 - 10)/2 = 2/2 = 1. One degree of unsaturation means the molecule contains exactly one ring or one pi bond — for example, a pentene or a cyclopentane.

ochem.q: Calculate the degrees of unsaturation for C6H5N (note: nitrogen contributes +1 in the numerator) using DoU = (2C + 2 + N - H - X)/2. What is the result, and what kind of structure could it represent?
opts: 4 (e.g., one aromatic ring + one C=N or one extra ring)
5 (e.g., aromatic ring + nitrile, like cyanobenzene C6H5CN minus C; in C6H5N a pyridine-like fused system)
ochem.why: DoU = (2(6) + 2 + 1 - 5)/2 = 10/2 = 5. Five degrees fit, for instance, an aromatic ring (4 DoU) plus an additional pi bond or ring. Always remember to add N in the numerator and subtract halogens.

ochem.q: An EI mass spectrum shows a molecular ion at m/z 78 with an M+2 peak at m/z 80 of nearly equal (~1:1) intensity. The natural-abundance isotope ratio identifies which halogen?
ochem.why: Bromine's two stable isotopes (79Br and 81Br) are nearly equally abundant, giving an M/M+2 doublet at ~1:1. Chlorine gives 3:1, and fluorine and iodine are monoisotopic (no M+2 from the halogen).

ochem.q: A 1H NMR of an unknown contains a singlet at 9.8 ppm integrating for one proton, plus a strong IR absorption at 1725 cm-1 and a band at 2720 cm-1. Which proton type is most consistent with the 9.8 ppm singlet?
ochem.why: Aldehyde protons resonate near 9.5-10 ppm because they are deshielded by the C=O group, and they often appear as a singlet (or weak doublet). The IR band at 2720 cm-1 (Fermi doublet with C-H stretch) plus 1725 cm-1 confirms an aldehyde.

ochem.q: An IR spectrum of an aromatic unknown shows two strong peaks at ~1530 cm-1 and ~1350 cm-1 (sometimes called the ‘vampire-tooth’ pair). Which substituent is most consistent with this pattern?
opts: Nitro group (NO2): asymmetric stretch ~1500-1570 + symmetric stretch ~1300-1380
ochem.why: Nitro groups have characteristic asymmetric and symmetric N-O stretches that appear as two strong bands near 1530 and 1350 cm-1. No other common group produces this distinctive ‘two-tooth’ pattern.

ochem.q: Diethyl ether (CH3CH2-O-CH2CH3) is a symmetric ether with four total carbons. How many distinct 13C NMR signals does it show, and why?
opts: 2 — the molecule has a mirror plane through the oxygen, so the two CH3's are equivalent and the two OCH2's are equivalent
ochem.why: Symmetric R-O-R molecules have a mirror plane through O. In diethyl ether the two methyl carbons are chemically equivalent and the two methylene carbons are equivalent, giving exactly two 13C signals.

ochem.q: An unknown is treated with Tollens reagent (Ag(NH3)2OH in dilute base) at room temperature. A silver mirror deposits on the inside of the test tube. Which functional group is being identified, and what is being oxidized?
opts: Aldehyde (oxidized to carboxylate; Ag+ reduced to Ag0)
Methyl ketone (Tollens does not oxidize ketones)
ochem.why: Tollens reagent is a mild oxidant that converts aldehydes (R-CHO) to carboxylates (R-COO-) while reducing the silver complex to elemental silver, which deposits as a mirror. Ketones lack the C-H on the carbonyl and don't react.

ochem.q: The iodoform test (I2 + aqueous NaOH) gives a yellow CHI3 precipitate. A positive result indicates the substrate contains either a CH3-C(=O)- group or a CH3-CH(OH)- group. Which class of compounds gives a positive iodoform test?
opts: Methyl ketones (and acetaldehyde) plus methyl carbinols (CH3-CH(OH)-R) that are oxidized in situ
All carbonyl compounds, including esters and amides
ochem.why: The iodoform reaction tri-iodinates the alpha-methyl of a methyl ketone (or methyl carbinol oxidized first). NaOH then cleaves the C-CI3 bond, releasing yellow CHI3 (iodoform). Substrates without a -COCH3 (or -CH(OH)CH3) cannot form CHI3.

ochem.q: Bromine in CCl4 (orange-red) is added dropwise to four separate samples in the dark. The orange color disappears within seconds for which substrate, indicating addition across the pi bond?
opts: Benzene (aromatic, requires Lewis acid catalyst for bromination)
ochem.why: Br2 in CCl4 undergoes electrophilic addition across alkene/alkyne pi bonds at room temperature without catalyst, consuming Br2 and decolorizing the solution. Alkanes need light/heat (radical), aromatics need Lewis acid, and alcohols don't react.

ochem.q: On a normal-phase TLC plate (silica = polar stationary phase) developed with a nonpolar mobile phase such as hexane/ethyl acetate (90:10), where does the most polar compound in a mixture end up after development?
opts: Travels furthest from the baseline (highest Rf)
Stays close to the baseline (lowest Rf) because it adsorbs strongly to the polar silica
ochem.why: ‘Like dissolves like’ on TLC: polar compounds bind tightly to polar silica and resist being carried along by a nonpolar solvent, giving low Rf values. Less polar species are pulled along with the solvent front and have higher Rf.

ochem.q: You need to separate two miscible organic liquids by simple distillation at atmospheric pressure. The technique works most cleanly when:
opts: Boiling points are within 5 degC of each other
Boiling points differ by more than ~25 degC, allowing the lower-boiling component to vaporize selectively
Both components have identical boiling points (azeotrope)
Neither liquid boils below its decomposition temperature
One is solid at room temperature
ochem.why: Simple distillation relies on a meaningful vapor-pressure difference. If the boiling points differ by less than ~25 degC, the vapor over the boiling mixture is too rich in both components and a fractional column is required for clean separation.

ochem.q: An ether solution contains both a carboxylic acid (pKa ~4) and a phenol (pKa ~10). To selectively pull only the carboxylic acid into the aqueous layer (leaving the phenol in ether), which aqueous wash is best?
opts: Saturated NaHCO3 (pKa of H2CO3 ~6.4): deprotonates the COOH (pKa 4) but not the phenol (pKa 10)
ochem.why: Bicarbonate is basic enough to deprotonate carboxylic acids (pKa ~4) but not phenols (pKa ~10), since the conjugate acid H2CO3 has pKa 6.4. Only the carboxylate is ionized and partitions into water, leaving the phenol in ether.

ochem.q: Recrystallization is the standard method for purifying a crystalline organic solid. Which choice best describes the procedure and the principle that delivers pure crystals?
opts: Boil away all of the solvent leaving the solid behind
Dissolve the impure solid in a minimum of hot solvent, then cool slowly so that the major component crystallizes selectively while small amounts of impurity remain in the cold mother liquor
Mix the solid with sand and filter
ochem.why: Recrystallization exploits the solubility difference between hot and cold solvent. Slow cooling allows the major (high-concentration) species to nucleate and form a clean crystal lattice, while trace impurities at low concentration remain dissolved and are washed away.

ochem.q: Gas chromatography (GC) separates volatile components passed through a heated column with a stationary phase. The primary physical property responsible for separation order is:
opts: Polarity alone, with no temperature dependence
Boiling point (volatility): lower-boiling components elute first because they spend less time in the liquid stationary phase
Molecular weight as the only determinant
ochem.why: GC separates by partitioning between mobile gas and the liquid stationary phase. Compounds with lower boiling points have higher vapor pressure, partition less into the stationary phase, and elute earlier. (Polarity matters only in the choice of stationary phase.)

ochem.q: Jones reagent (CrO3 in aqueous H2SO4/acetone) is added to 2-pentanol (a secondary alcohol) at 0 degC. The major product is:
opts: 2-pentanone (a ketone) — Jones cleanly oxidizes 2 deg alcohols to ketones
Pentanoic acid (over-oxidation product, requires 1 deg alcohol)
ochem.why: Secondary alcohols have only one alpha hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, so oxidation stops at the ketone. Jones cannot oxidize a 2 deg alcohol further (no remaining alpha-H). Primary alcohols, in contrast, would go all the way to the carboxylic acid under aqueous Jones.

ochem.q: 1-butanol is independently treated with (a) PCC in dry CH2Cl2 and (b) Jones reagent (CrO3/H2SO4 aq). Which reagent stops cleanly at the aldehyde, and why?
opts: PCC — anhydrous, mild Cr(VI) reagent that cannot form the aldehyde hydrate, so no over-oxidation to carboxylic acid
Neither — both go to the acid
ochem.why: Over-oxidation of an aldehyde requires hydration of the C=O to a gem-diol, which Cr(VI) then re-oxidizes to a carboxylic acid. PCC is run in anhydrous CH2Cl2, so the aldehyde never hydrates and the reaction halts cleanly. Jones is aqueous and proceeds to the acid.

ochem.q: An ether solution contains a carboxylic acid (pKa ~4), a phenol (pKa ~10), and aniline (an aromatic amine, conjugate acid pKa ~4.6). After washing with saturated aqueous NaHCO3, which compound remains in the ether layer?
opts: Carboxylic acid (it's deprotonated and pulled into water)
Phenol (NaHCO3 is too weak a base to deprotonate phenol, pKa 10, so phenol stays in ether)
Aniline (it's a base; NaHCO3 wouldn't ionize it anyway, but the question asks who NaHCO3 leaves behind — both phenol and aniline stay; among the listed single answers, phenol is the cleanest)
All three end up in the aqueous layer
All three remain in the ether layer
ochem.why: NaHCO3 (conjugate acid pKa 6.4) deprotonates the carboxylic acid (pKa 4) and pulls it into water, but it's too weak to deprotonate the phenol (pKa 10). The neutral phenol stays in ether. Aniline is a base and is unaffected by bicarbonate, so it also stays in ether.

ochem.q: A Diels-Alder cycloaddition is run between a 1,3-diene and an electron-poor dienophile in toluene at 80 degC. Which conformation must the diene adopt to undergo the [4+2], and why is the alternative geometrically forbidden?
opts: s-trans, because the termini are far apart
s-cis, so the two terminal carbons can simultaneously bond to the two dienophile carbons in a single concerted pericyclic step
ochem.why: Diels-Alder is a concerted suprafacial-suprafacial [4+2] requiring both ends of the diene to reach the dienophile at once. Only the s-cis conformer places those termini close enough; s-trans is too elongated.

ochem.q: 1,3-butadiene reacts with maleic anhydride (a strong dienophile) in xylene at reflux. Predict the product and the relative stereochemistry, considering the suprafacial-suprafacial nature of the Diels-Alder cycloaddition.
opts: An open-chain ester with cis double bonds
cis-4-cyclohexene-1,2-dicarboxylic anhydride (the two anhydride substituents end up cis on the new six-membered ring; endo selectivity favored)
ochem.why: Diels-Alder is a syn (suprafacial) addition on both partners, so the two anhydride substituents on maleic anhydride remain cis on the newly formed cyclohexene ring. The C=C between C4-C5 of the new ring is retained.

ochem.q: Cold, dilute aqueous KMnO4 (basic conditions, ~0 degC) is added to cyclohexene. The major organic product is:
opts: cis-cyclohexane-1,2-diol (a syn diol from concerted [3+2] addition of MnO4-)
ochem.why: Cold, dilute KMnO4 forms a cyclic manganate ester across one face of the alkene, then hydrolyzes to deliver both OH groups to the same face — a syn-diol. Hot/concentrated KMnO4 instead cleaves to carbonyls.

ochem.q: 2-methyl-2-butene is treated with O3 in CH2Cl2 at -78 degC, then with Zn/AcOH (reductive workup). Identify the two carbonyl products formed by cleavage across the trisubstituted alkene.
opts: Acetone + acetaldehyde (the more substituted side gives a ketone; the less substituted side gives an aldehyde)
Two molecules of acetic acid (oxidative workup)
ochem.why: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C, replacing each carbon's substituents with =O. The 2-substituted side (CMe2) becomes acetone; the 3-CH(CH3) side becomes acetaldehyde. Reductive workup (Zn/AcOH or Me2S) prevents oxidation of the aldehyde.

ochem.q: Cyclohexene is treated with N-bromosuccinimide (NBS) in CCl4 with a low constant concentration of Br2 (radical chain) under hv at room temperature. Identify the regiochemistry of the bromine atom in the major product.
opts: Br adds across both alkene carbons (1,2-dibromide)
Br is installed at the allylic position (C3, next to C=C); the alkene is preserved
Br ends up on a random vinyl carbon
No reaction without a Lewis acid catalyst
ochem.why: NBS/hv generates a low concentration of Br• that selectively abstracts the weakest C-H — the allylic position, giving a resonance-stabilized allyl radical. The radical then traps Br• to form 3-bromocyclohexene; the C=C is retained.

ochem.q: 1-methylcyclohexene is subjected to hydroboration-oxidation: BH3·THF at 0 degC, then aqueous NaOH/H2O2. What is the major alcohol, including stereochemistry?
opts: 1-methylcyclohexanol (Markovnikov OH at the more substituted C)
trans-2-methylcyclohexanol (anti-Markovnikov OH on the less hindered C, syn addition of B and H places OH and CH3 trans)
ochem.why: Hydroboration is anti-Markovnikov (boron goes to the less substituted C) and syn (B and H on the same face). Oxidative workup retains stereochemistry, replacing B with OH. On 1-methylcyclohexene this places OH on C2 trans to the C1 methyl.

ochem.q: 2-pentyne is hydrogenated using H2 over Lindlar's catalyst (Pd/CaCO3 poisoned with Pb(OAc)2 and quinoline) in EtOAc at 1 atm. The major product is:
opts: (Z)-2-pentene (cis alkene; H2 delivered syn from one face of the surface and the reduction halts at the alkene)
An equilibrium mixture of cis and trans alkenes
ochem.why: Lindlar is a deactivated Pd catalyst that delivers H2 syn to the same face of the alkyne and is poisoned enough that further reduction of the alkene is suppressed. The result is a Z (cis) alkene.

ochem.q: 2-pentyne is treated with sodium metal in liquid ammonia at -33 degC. After workup, the major alkene product is:
opts: (E)-2-pentene (trans, from dissolving-metal reduction via radical anion intermediate)
ochem.why: Dissolving-metal reduction (Na/NH3(l)) proceeds through a vinyl radical anion that adopts the more stable trans geometry before being protonated by ammonia. The result is a stereospecifically E (trans) alkene.

ochem.q: An aldehyde is stirred with two equivalents of methanol in the presence of a catalytic acid (p-TsOH) under Dean-Stark conditions to remove water. Which functional group is the final isolated product?
opts: Acetal (R-CH(OMe)2, sp3 C bonded to two -OMe groups)
ochem.why: Acid-catalyzed addition of one equivalent of ROH gives the hemiacetal; loss of water (driven by the Dean-Stark trap) and a second ROH addition installs the second alkoxy group, yielding an acetal. Acetals are stable under base and serve as carbonyl protecting groups.

ochem.q: Cyclohexanone is treated with pyrrolidine (a secondary amine) and a catalytic amount of p-TsOH in benzene at reflux with a Dean-Stark trap. The product is:
opts: An enamine (the nitrogen is bonded to the alpha-carbon analog; pi bond between alpha-C and former carbonyl C)
ochem.why: Secondary amines lack a second N-H, so the iminium intermediate cannot tautomerize to a neutral C=N. Instead, an alpha-proton is lost to form a C=C-N enamine, with water removed by Dean-Stark.

ochem.q: Acetophenone (PhCOCH3) is heated with one equivalent of methylamine (a primary amine) in benzene with catalytic AcOH and a Dean-Stark trap to remove water. Identify the major product.
opts: Imine (Schiff base): PhC(=NMe)CH3, formed by condensation and loss of H2O
ochem.why: Primary amines have two N-H bonds. After nucleophilic addition gives the hemiaminal, water is eliminated and the second N-H is lost to give a neutral C=N (imine, Schiff base). Secondary amines instead form enamines.

ochem.q: Sodium borohydride (NaBH4) in methanol at 0 degC is added to a flask containing one of each functional group below. Which subset of carbonyls does NaBH4 reduce, and which does it leave untouched?
opts: Reduces aldehydes, ketones, and acid chlorides cleanly; does NOT reduce esters, carboxylic acids, or amides
ochem.why: NaBH4 is a mild hydride source: strong enough to attack highly electrophilic C=O of aldehydes, ketones, and acid chlorides, but too weak for esters, amides, and carboxylic acids (which need LiAlH4). It tolerates protic solvents like methanol.

ochem.q: A primary amide R-C(=O)NH2 is reduced with excess LiAlH4 in dry diethyl ether at 0 degC, then aqueous workup. The product is:
opts: Aldehyde R-CHO (would require a milder controlled reduction such as DIBAL at -78 degC)
Alcohol R-CH2-OH (this is the LiAlH4 product of an ester or acid)
ochem.why: LiAlH4 reduces amides all the way to amines: hydride attacks C=O, the nitrogen pushes out -O- to give an iminium, and a second hydride reduces the iminium to a CH2-NR group. Net: -C(=O)-NR2 -> -CH2-NR2.

ochem.q: Phenylmagnesium bromide (PhMgBr) is added to acetonitrile (CH3CN) in dry ether at 0 degC, then the reaction mixture is treated with aqueous H3O+. The final product is:
opts: An aryl alkyl ketone (PhCOCH3, acetophenone) — addition gives an N-magnesiomide that hydrolyzes to a ketone on aqueous workup
ochem.why: Grignards add once to nitriles, giving an N-Mg ketimine intermediate. Aqueous acidic workup hydrolyzes the imine to a ketone. The carbon from the nitrile becomes the carbonyl carbon, and the alkyl/aryl from the nitrile becomes one substituent.

ochem.q: Methylenetriphenylphosphorane (Ph3P=CH2, an unstabilized Wittig ylide) is added to cyclohexanone in THF at room temperature. Identify the products.
opts: An alkene (methylenecyclohexane) plus triphenylphosphine oxide (Ph3P=O); Wittig replaces C=O with C=C
ochem.why: The Wittig reaction joins the carbonyl carbon to the ylide carbon and ejects the oxygen as Ph3P=O via a four-membered oxaphosphetane, replacing C=O with C=C. Unstabilized ylides typically give the Z-alkene; on a ketone like cyclohexanone, geometry doesn't apply.

ochem.q: A weak (soft) nucleophile such as a cuprate or a stabilized enolate is added to methyl vinyl ketone (CH2=CH-C(=O)CH3) at -78 degC. Which carbon does it attack, and what is this regiochemistry called?
opts: The alpha carbon (between the carbonyl and the beta carbon)
The beta carbon (1,4-/conjugate/Michael addition); soft nucleophiles are reversible at C=O and prefer the thermodynamic conjugate adduct
ochem.why: Hard nucleophiles (RLi, RMgX) attack the carbonyl carbon in a 1,2-fashion; soft nucleophiles add reversibly at C=O but irreversibly at the beta carbon (1,4-addition, Michael). The resulting enolate then tautomerizes to the saturated ketone.

ochem.q: 2-methylcyclohexanone has two distinct alpha positions. It is treated with one equivalent of LDA in THF at -78 degC. Which enolate predominates, and what is the principle?
opts: The thermodynamic (more substituted) enolate, because it is more stable
The kinetic (less substituted) enolate, because LDA is a bulky, strong, non-nucleophilic base that selectively removes the more accessible (less hindered) alpha-H at low temperature
ochem.why: LDA's large isopropyl groups disfavor abstraction of a hindered alpha-H. At -78 degC the kinetic deprotonation is locked in (no equilibration), giving the less-substituted (kinetic) enolate. Higher T or weaker bases give the more stable thermodynamic enolate.

ochem.q: Which substrate gives a positive iodoform test (yellow CHI3 precipitate) when treated with I2 and aqueous NaOH at 0 degC?
opts: A methyl ketone (R-COCH3) or methyl carbinol (R-CH(OH)CH3) — base-catalyzed alpha-iodination of the CH3 followed by hydroxide cleavage of the C-CI3 bond
ochem.why: The iodoform reaction tri-iodinates the alpha methyl, then NaOH cleaves the C-CI3 bond to give a carboxylate plus yellow CHI3. Only -COCH3 (methyl ketones, acetaldehyde) or methyl carbinols (which oxidize first under the conditions) qualify.

ochem.q: An aldol reaction between two molecules of acetaldehyde (NaOH, H2O) is heated above 60 degC. Beyond the initial beta-hydroxy aldehyde, what is the dehydration product?
opts: alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl (enone/enal); E1cb dehydration eliminates water across alpha-beta to give the conjugated product (crotonaldehyde here)
ochem.why: Heating an aldol drives E1cb dehydration: the alpha-H is removed (acidic due to the new beta-OH adjacent C=O), and -OH leaves, giving conjugation between C=C and C=O — an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl. Conjugation provides the thermodynamic driving force.

ochem.q: Two equivalents of ethyl acetate are treated with sodium ethoxide in dry ethanol, then quenched with aqueous acid. Identify the type of product formed by this Claisen condensation.
opts: A beta-keto ester (ethyl acetoacetate, CH3COCH2COOEt) — one ester's enolate displaces the OEt of a second ester
ochem.why: In a Claisen, an alpha-deprotonated ester attacks the carbonyl of a second ester; the alkoxide (-OEt) then leaves, yielding a beta-keto ester. The product is acidic (pKa ~11) and is deprotonated by ethoxide, driving equilibrium forward.

ochem.q: Ethyl acetoacetate (CH3COCH2COOEt) is treated with NaOEt, then ethyl iodide, then aqueous NaOH (saponification), then heat. The acetoacetic ester synthesis builds substituted:
opts: Methyl ketones (the final beta-keto acid loses CO2 via a 6-membered TS, leaving R-CH2-COCH3)
Carboxylic acids (that's the malonic ester synthesis)
ochem.why: Acetoacetic ester synthesis: alkylate the central CH2, then saponify the ester to a beta-keto acid that decarboxylates on heat (6-membered TS) — leaving a methyl ketone bearing the new R group at the alpha carbon.

ochem.q: Diethyl malonate (CH2(COOEt)2) is treated with NaOEt, then n-propyl iodide, then aqueous NaOH (saponification), then heat. The malonic ester synthesis builds substituted:
opts: Carboxylic acids — the resulting malonic acid loses one CO2 via a 6-membered TS, leaving a single -COOH bearing the new alkyl group
ochem.why: Malonic ester synthesis: alkylate the central CH2 (pKa ~13 due to flanking esters), saponify both esters to a malonic diacid, and heat. One -COOH decarboxylates via a 6-membered TS, leaving R-CH2-COOH — a substituted carboxylic acid.

ochem.q: A beta-keto acid (e.g., acetoacetic acid, CH3COCH2COOH) is heated to ~120 degC in an inert solvent. What is the principal transformation, and what is the geometric requirement?
opts: Decarboxylation to lose CO2 via a six-membered cyclic transition state in which the carboxylic O-H is shuttled to the carbonyl oxygen, forming an enol that tautomerizes to a methyl ketone (acetone)
ochem.why: The beta-keto group is positioned to accept the -COOH proton through a six-membered TS, allowing concerted loss of CO2 and formation of an enol. The enol tautomerizes to the more stable keto form. This is why acetoacetic and malonic ester syntheses end with heat.

ochem.q: A molecule contains three stereogenic centers and no internal symmetry (no meso form). Using 2^n, what is the MAXIMUM possible number of distinct stereoisomers?
ochem.why: Each stereocenter contributes a factor of 2 (R or S), so the maximum count is 2^n. With n=3 centers and no symmetry to fold pairs into meso compounds, the molecule has 2^3 = 8 distinct stereoisomers (4 pairs of enantiomers).

ochem.q: Tartaric acid has two stereogenic centers but only three stereoisomers total. The third compound is called the meso form. Which statement best characterizes a meso compound?
opts: Achiral overall despite containing stereogenic centers, due to an internal mirror plane (the two halves are mirror images of each other within the same molecule)
ochem.why: A meso compound contains stereocenters but is superimposable on its mirror image because of an internal mirror plane. The local rotations cancel and the molecule is optically inactive — different from a racemate, which is a 1:1 mixture of two enantiomers.

ochem.q: A solution contains a 50:50 mixture of (R)- and (S)-2-bromobutane (a racemic mixture). Light from a sodium D line (589 nm) is passed through a polarimeter cell of fixed length. The observed optical rotation is:
opts: 0 deg, because equal and opposite contributions cancel
ochem.why: Each enantiomer rotates plane-polarized light by an equal magnitude in opposite directions. With equal concentrations (50:50), the rotations cancel exactly, giving an observed rotation of 0 — the defining feature of a racemic mixture.

ochem.q: (Z)- and (E)-2-butene differ only in the spatial arrangement around the C=C double bond. They are not mirror images of each other. The most accurate classification of this stereochemical relationship is:
opts: Diastereomers (stereoisomers that are not mirror images)
ochem.why: Cis (Z) and trans (E) alkene isomers have identical connectivity but different spatial arrangements; they are not mirror images of each other (each is achiral). Stereoisomers that are not enantiomers are diastereomers — and they have different physical properties.

ochem.q: On a Fischer projection, the lowest CIP priority group (often H) is on a horizontal line, which means it points TOWARD the viewer. Reading priorities 1->2->3 traces out a clockwise circle on paper. What is the true R/S designation, and why?
opts: S, because the lowest priority points toward you, so you must invert the apparent rotation
Cannot be determined from a Fischer projection
ochem.why: CIP requires the lowest-priority group to point AWAY from the viewer. If it points toward you, the directly read rotation is reversed: clockwise on paper actually corresponds to S, and counterclockwise corresponds to R.

ochem.q: Two diastereomers of a chiral natural product are isolated. Compared with each other, which physical/chemical properties typically differ?
opts: Only the sign of optical rotation; everything else is identical
Most physical properties — boiling point, melting point, solubility, density, IR/NMR — and reactivity, because diastereomers are not mirror images and have different internal energies
Only the wavelength of UV absorption
ochem.why: Diastereomers differ in spatial arrangement but are not mirror images, so their internal interactions (steric, dipole, H-bonding) differ. That gives different boiling/melting points, solubilities, NMR shifts, and even different reaction rates — unlike enantiomers, which differ only in chiral environments.

ochem.q: Hückel's rule states a flat, fully-conjugated, cyclic system is aromatic when it has 4n+2 pi electrons. Cyclobutadiene is square planar, fully conjugated, and has 4 pi electrons. How is cyclobutadiene best classified, and what does that imply for its stability?
opts: Anti-aromatic (4 pi electrons, 4n with n=1) and destabilized — even less stable than the open-chain analog
Aromatic but only at low temperature
ochem.why: A planar, fully conjugated cyclic system with 4n pi electrons (here 4) is anti-aromatic by Hückel's rule. Cyclobutadiene is destabilized relative to its non-cyclic dienyl reference — it actually distorts to a rectangular geometry to minimize anti-aromatic destabilization.

ochem.q: Nitrobenzene (PhNO2) is treated with Br2/FeBr3 at 0 degC. The nitro group is a strong sigma-withdrawing AND pi-withdrawing substituent. Where does the new Br substituent end up, and why?
opts: Meta (1,3-disposition); the NO2 destabilizes the ortho/para sigma-complex by placing positive charge directly on the carbon bearing -NO2
ochem.why: Strongly deactivating substituents (NO2, CN, COR, COOH, SO3H, NR3+) destabilize the arenium ion when the new substituent goes ortho or para — the cation rests on a carbon bearing the EWG. The meta product avoids that, so EAS is meta-selective (and slow).

ochem.q: Nitrobenzene is treated with acetyl chloride and AlCl3 (standard Friedel-Crafts acylation conditions) in CH2Cl2 at 0 degC. What is the result?
opts: No reaction — the strongly deactivating -NO2 makes the ring too electron-poor for Friedel-Crafts (acylation OR alkylation) to proceed
Yes, but only at high temperature (>200 degC)
Forms an N,N-acyl product on the nitrogen
ochem.why: Friedel-Crafts reactions fail on rings bearing strong deactivators (-NO2, -CN, -SO3H, -NR3+, -CF3) because the ring is too electron-poor to attack the acylium ion. They also fail on -NH2 rings because the amine ties up AlCl3 (Lewis acid quenching).

ochem.q: Halogens (-F, -Cl, -Br, -I) are unusual EAS substituents because they show one effect inductively and the opposite effect through resonance. In EAS bromination of chlorobenzene, the regiochemistry and rate are best described as:
opts: Deactivate (-I dominates rate) but direct ortho/para (+M lone pair stabilizes the sigma-complex when the new group is ortho/para)
ochem.why: Halogens are sigma-withdrawing through induction (slowing the reaction) but pi-donating through resonance via the lone pair (giving ortho/para selectivity). The two effects partially cancel, so halobenzenes react in EAS slower than benzene but with ortho/para regiochemistry.

ochem.q: An aryl diazonium salt (ArN2+ Cl-) prepared at 0 degC from an aniline + NaNO2/HCl is treated with CuBr (a Sandmeyer reagent). The major product is:
opts: Ar-Br (Sandmeyer: copper(I) bromide replaces -N2+ with -Br via radical mechanism)
ochem.why: Sandmeyer reactions use Cu(I) salts to replace -N2+ on the ring: CuBr -> ArBr; CuCl -> ArCl; CuCN -> ArCN. They proceed via a single-electron transfer mechanism that releases N2 gas. CuI does not work — KI is used instead.

ochem.q: Toluene (PhCH3) is heated with hot, concentrated KMnO4 (aqueous, ~100 degC) for several hours and then acidified. What is the organic product?
opts: Benzoic acid (PhCOOH); side-chain oxidation cleaves all benzylic C-H bonds and installs a -COOH directly on the ring
ochem.why: Hot KMnO4 oxidizes any alkyl group with at least one benzylic C-H all the way to a carboxylic acid attached directly to the ring, regardless of original chain length. Tert-butyl groups (no benzylic H) are inert. Toluene -> benzoic acid.

ochem.why: IR at 1715 cm−1 with no broad O-H stretch confirms a ketone. The 1H NMR shows a triplet at 1.06 ppm (3H, CH3), a singlet at 2.13 ppm (3H, CH3CO), and a quartet at 2.45 ppm (2H, CH2). This three-signal pattern with those integrations matches 2-pentanone (methyl propyl ketone): CH3-CO-CH2CH2CH3, where the terminal methyl and adjacent CH2 give the triplet/quartet, and the acetyl CH3 gives the singlet.

ortho- and meta-nitrotoluene; methyl is a deactivator
ochem.why: CH3 is an activating ortho/para director via hyperconjugation. Nitration gives ~60% para and ~40% ortho with traces of meta.

ochem.q: A compound with the structure (2R, 3S)-2,3-dichlorobutane is heated. Its mirror image is (2S, 3R)-2,3-dichlorobutane. Which statement correctly describes the relationship between these two molecules and any internal symmetry?

They are diastereomers; they have different physical properties
They are the SAME meso compound; the internal mirror plane makes the molecule achiral and optically inactive
They are constitutional isomers; the connectivity differs
They are conformers; rotation around C2-C3 interconverts them
ochem.why: (2R,3S) has an internal mirror plane between C2 and C3 that swaps R↔S → meso. The "mirror image" is identical to itself; meso compounds are achiral despite having stereocenters.

ochem.q: Propose a 3-step synthesis of 2-methylpentan-2-ol starting from 2-bromopropane. Step 1: Mg, dry ether. Step 2: react with X. Step 3: aqueous workup. What is reagent X?
ochem.why: Step 1 makes isopropylmagnesium bromide. Adding it to butan-2-one (CH3COCH2CH3) gives a tertiary alcohol: HO-C(CH3)(C(CH3)2H)CH2CH3 = 2-methylpentan-2-ol after workup. Acetone would give 2,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol; propanal would give a secondary alcohol.

ochem.q: 2-chloro-2,3-dimethylbutane is dissolved in 80% ethanol/20% water and gently warmed. The reaction follows first-order kinetics. Among the products is a tertiary alcohol that is NOT the simple substitution product of the original carbon. Which mechanism best explains this observation?
opts: SN2 with backside displacement on the secondary carbon
SN1 with a 1,2-methyl shift forming a more stable tertiary carbocation, then water attack
E1cb deprotonation generating an enolate intermediate
Direct radical-chain substitution via a chlorine radical
ochem.why: First-order kinetics + tertiary halide + protic solvent = SN1. The initial 3° cation can undergo 1,2-methyl shift to give an even more stable cation; water attack at the new center yields a rearranged tertiary alcohol.

ochem.q: Two molecules of acetone undergo a base-catalyzed self-aldol condensation followed by dehydration upon heating. The aqueous NaOH first deprotonates an alpha hydrogen; the resulting enolate attacks the carbonyl of a second acetone molecule. What is the major final product after dehydration?
ochem.why: Self-aldol of acetone: enolate of one acetone attacks the carbonyl of another → 4-hydroxy-4-methylpentan-2-one. Heat drives dehydration of the β-hydroxy ketone to the α,β-unsaturated ketone mesityl oxide.

ochem.q: You compare the 13C NMR spectra of two C8H10 isomers: para-xylene and ortho-xylene. Based purely on molecular symmetry, how many UNIQUE carbon environments would each compound exhibit?
ochem.why: p-xylene has D2h symmetry: the two ring carbons bearing CH3 are equivalent, the four other ring carbons are pairwise equivalent (2), and the two methyls are equivalent (1) → 3 unique. o-xylene has C2v symmetry: 4 unique aromatic environments + 1 unique methyl = 4 unique total. Higher symmetry → fewer peaks.

ochem.q: Rank the following four amines in order of DECREASING basicity in aqueous solution: pyridine, aniline, ammonia, and triethylamine.
ochem.why: Aliphatic 3° amine (Et3N, pKaH ~10.7) > NH3 (pKaH ~9.25) > pyridine (pKaH ~5.2, sp2 N pulls lone pair into the ring) > aniline (pKaH ~4.6, lone pair conjugates into the aromatic ring).

ochem.q: A chemist performs Friedel-Crafts alkylation of benzene using tert-butyl chloride and AlCl3 to make tert-butylbenzene. The reaction works in good yield. However, when the same chemist attempts the same reaction on nitrobenzene, no product forms even after extended heating. Which factor best explains the failure?
opts: The nitro group strongly deactivates the ring (resonance withdrawal); the resulting arenium intermediate cannot form
The nitro group reacts preferentially with AlCl3, consuming the Lewis acid
Friedel-Crafts alkylation requires alkenes, not alkyl halides
tert-butyl cation rearranges before substitution can occur
ochem.why: Nitro is a strong −M deactivator. It depletes electron density from the ring and destabilizes the arenium (sigma-complex) intermediate so much that Friedel-Crafts alkylation effectively fails.

ochem.q: A student isolates a mixture of benzoic acid (pKa ≈ 4.2), 2-naphthol (pKa ≈ 9.5), and naphthalene (neutral) in dichloromethane. They wish to separate all three using acid-base extraction with two aqueous solutions. Which order of washes correctly extracts the carboxylic acid first and the phenol second?
opts: Wash 1: 1 M NaOH (extracts both); wash 2: 1 M HCl (re-extracts phenol)
Wash 1: saturated NaHCO3 (extracts carboxylic acid only); wash 2: 1 M NaOH (extracts phenol)
Wash 1: 1 M HCl (extracts amine); wash 2: saturated NaHCO3 (extracts phenol)
Wash 1: saturated NaCl (salts out carboxylic acid); wash 2: NaOH (extracts naphthalene)
Wash 1: 1 M NaOH (extracts naphthalene); wash 2: 1 M HCl (extracts both acids)
ochem.why: NaHCO3 deprotonates carboxylic acids (pKa < 6) but not phenols (pKa ~10). NaOH then deprotonates the phenol. Naphthalene stays in DCM.

ochem.q: A Diels-Alder reaction is performed between (E,E)-2,4-hexadiene and maleic anhydride. The reaction is concerted, suprafacial on both components, and proceeds through a single cyclic transition state. Which statement about the stereochemistry of the cyclohexene product is CORRECT?
opts: The two methyl groups end up trans on the cyclohexene ring; the anhydride carbonyls are syn (endo)
The two methyl groups end up cis on the cyclohexene ring; the anhydride is also cis to them (endo)
All substituents end up trans; this is a [4+2] anti-suprafacial process
The product is a 1:1 mixture of cis and trans methyl groups
The reaction does not proceed because (E,E)-dienes cannot reach the s-cis conformation
ochem.why: Concerted Diels-Alder preserves dienophile and diene stereochemistry: (E,E)-diene gives cis methyls on the new ring; maleic anhydride (cis dienophile) gives cis ester groups; endo rule typically dominates kinetically.

ochem.q: (2S,3S)-3-bromo-2-butanol is treated with concentrated HBr at 50 °C. The product is identified as (2S,3R)-2,3-dibromobutane (a meso compound). Which mechanism best accounts for both the regiochemistry and the loss of optical activity?
opts: SN2 with backside attack at C2 inverting that center while C3 is unchanged
SN1 via a bridged bromonium ion at C2-C3 followed by anti-periplanar attack of Br⁻ at C2
Pinacol rearrangement followed by Br⁻ capture
Two sequential SN2 steps with double inversion
ochem.why: Neighboring-group participation by Br at C3 forms a bridged bromonium intermediate. Br⁻ opens it from the backside at C2, inverting C2 and giving the (2S,3R) meso diastereomer.

ochem.q: A compound with molecular formula C₉H₁₀O₂ shows: IR 1715 cm⁻¹ (no broad O–H); ¹H NMR singlet 3.85 ppm (3H), AA'BB' pattern 7.85 (2H) and 6.92 (2H), singlet 2.55 (3H); ¹³C shows 5 unique aromatic carbons. Identify the compound.
ochem.why: Para substitution → AA'BB' aromatic pattern (4 H total appearing as two doublets). 1715 cm⁻¹ is methyl ketone, not ester (esters ~1735–1745). The 3.85-ppm OMe singlet + 2.55 ppm methyl ketone fit p-methoxyacetophenone (DOU=5; 5 unique aromatic C's due to p-symmetry).

ochem.q: A chemist needs meta-bromonitrobenzene from benzene. Two single-step routes are tried: (i) Br₂/FeBr₃ then HNO₃/H₂SO₄, or (ii) HNO₃/H₂SO₄ then Br₂/FeBr₃. Which gives the desired meta isomer in good yield, and why does the other route fail?
opts: (i) works; the methyl ortho/para directs nitration meta
(ii) works; nitro is a meta director, so subsequent bromination installs Br meta
Neither works; meta-bromonitrobenzene must be made via diazonium chemistry
(i) works because Br is a meta director; (ii) fails because nitrobenzene cannot brominate
ochem.why: Install the strong meta director (NO₂) FIRST. Subsequent bromination of nitrobenzene proceeds (slowly) at the meta position. Route (i) installs Br first (an ortho/para director), so nitration ends up ortho/para to Br rather than meta.

ochem.q: A symmetric ketone is treated with LDA (1 equiv) at −78 °C in THF, then methyl iodide is added. Workup gives an alpha-methylated ketone with high regioselectivity for the LESS substituted alpha carbon (kinetic enolate). Which combination of features explains why LDA at low T gives the kinetic product instead of the thermodynamic one?
opts: LDA is small and nucleophilic; it adds to the carbonyl rather than removes the alpha proton
LDA is sterically bulky and a strong, non-nucleophilic base; low T prevents enolate equilibration to the more stable substituted enolate
LDA generates radicals that abstract H from the less hindered C
Low T accelerates the more-substituted enolate formation via tunneling
LDA is acidic, protonating the more-substituted alpha C
ochem.why: Bulky, non-nucleophilic base + low T → rapid, irreversible deprotonation at the most accessible alpha H = kinetic enolate at the less substituted side. Thermodynamic conditions (NaH, room T) would give the more substituted enolate.

ochem.q: A molecule has three stereocenters and ONE internal mirror plane that bisects the central C and exchanges the other two stereocenters. How many distinct stereoisomers does the molecule have, and how many of them are optically active?
opts: 4 total (one of which is meso); 2 optically active
ochem.why: Internal mirror plane reduces 2³ = 8 to 4 unique configurations. Pairs related by the mirror plane collapse: (RRR ↔ SSS pair active enantiomers), (RSR = meso, achiral), (SRS = meso, achiral). So 4 distinct stereoisomers, 2 optically active.

ochem.q: Compare the gas-phase acidity (deprotonation energy) of CH₃CO₂H and CF₃CO₂H to their aqueous-phase acidity (pKa). In which phase is the inductive effect of the −CF₃ group MORE dominant in determining the relative acidity, and why?
opts: Aqueous phase; water solvation amplifies the inductive effect
Gas phase; without solvent, the only stabilization of the conjugate base is intrinsic (inductive/resonance), so the substituent effect is larger in magnitude
Both phases are equally affected — pKa differences mirror gas-phase ΔE
Inductive effects only operate in the gas phase; in water they vanish
Aqueous phase; the trifluoromethyl group H-bonds to water
ochem.why: In the gas phase the conjugate base has no solvation, so substituent stabilization (inductive of CF₃) dominates the ΔE. In solution, water stabilizes the carboxylate so much that intrinsic substituent effects are partially leveled — hence smaller pKa differences than gas-phase trends would suggest.

ochem.q: Treatment of (E)-2-butene with mCPBA followed by aqueous acid yields one diastereomer of 2,3-butanediol almost exclusively. Identify the product and the stereochemical reason.
opts: (2R,3S) meso compound; epoxide opens with anti (trans) addition of OH groups, giving overall syn-addition appearance from a trans-alkene
(2R,3R)/(2S,3S) racemate; trans-alkene → trans-diol via concerted syn epoxidation followed by anti opening
A single optically active enantiomer; mCPBA is chiral
ochem.why: mCPBA epoxidizes (E)-2-butene to a (2R,3R) / (2S,3S) trans-epoxide racemate. Acid opens the epoxide via SN2-like backside attack of water → anti opening; combined with the trans starting material the net diol is the (2R,3R)/(2S,3S) racemate (both stereocenters inverted at one carbon).

ochem.q: In an SN1 solvolysis of 3-chloro-3-methyl-1-butene in aqueous ethanol, two products form: 3-methyl-3-buten-2-ol and 2-methyl-3-buten-2-ol, in roughly 60:40 ratio. What best explains the formation of BOTH products from the same intermediate?
opts: A single allylic carbocation is delocalized across two carbons; nucleophile attacks at either resonance position
A radical chain mechanism with two propagation pathways
The starting material isomerizes before ionization
Carbocation rearrangement via methyl shift forms a new structure entirely
ochem.why: Ionization gives an allylic cation with positive character on both ends of the π-system. Water attack at either resonance center gives the two regioisomeric alcohols.

ochem.q: You need to synthesize a compound containing exactly ONE primary alcohol AND ONE tertiary alcohol on the same skeleton, starting from acetone and an alkyl Grignard. Which 3-step strategy works and gives high yield?
opts: (1) Grignard adds to acetone → tertiary alcohol; (2) protect with TMS-Cl/imidazole; (3) hydroboration-oxidation of a separate alkene to install the primary OH; deprotect.
Open an epoxide with the Grignard (gives 1° alcohol on one chain) then add the resulting Mg-alkoxide intramolecularly to acetone for the 3° alcohol — single pot.
Cannot be done — Grignards are basic and would deprotonate any alcohol formed
Reduce acetone to 2-propanol with NaBH4, then etherify to install primary alcohol
ochem.why: Sequence: Grignard → 3° alcohol; protect; install 1° alcohol via independent hydroboration-oxidation; deprotect. The protection step is mandatory — Grignards or strong bases would otherwise destroy alcohols formed earlier.

ochem.q: Which compound shows the LARGEST chemical-shift downfield (highest ppm) for the indicated proton in ¹H NMR? Choose the proton that experiences the strongest deshielding from a combination of electronegativity, anisotropy, and resonance-induced positive character.
opts: The carboxylic-acid OH of acetic acid (δ ~12)
ochem.why: Carboxylic acid O–H typically appears as a very broad signal at 11–13 ppm — by far the most deshielded common proton due to strong H-bonding plus the electron-poor O. Aldehydic H is next (~9.7).

ochem.q: In acidic aqueous solution at pH 1, which compound exists predominantly as its CATIONIC conjugate-acid form? (Use approximate pKaH: pyridine 5.2, aniline 4.6, methylamine 10.6, imidazole 7.0, pyrrole −3.8.)
opts: Methylamine, pyridine, aniline, imidazole — all four protonated; pyrrole remains neutral
Only methylamine is protonated; the others are neutral at pH 1
All five compounds are protonated at pH 1
Aniline alone is protonated; the rest are too weakly basic
Pyrrole and pyridine are protonated; methylamine and aniline are not
ochem.why: A base is mostly protonated when pH < pKaH. At pH 1: methylamine (10.6 ✓), imidazole (7.0 ✓), pyridine (5.2 ✓), aniline (4.6 ✓) are all protonated. Pyrrole (pKaH = −3.8) requires pH < −3.8 to protonate, so it stays neutral.

ochem.q: A student runs TLC of a mixture of three compounds: a carboxylic acid, an alcohol, and a hydrocarbon. They use silica gel (polar stationary phase) with hexane:ethyl acetate (4:1) as the mobile phase. Which compound has the LARGEST Rf value (travels furthest), and why?
opts: Carboxylic acid; it ionizes and elutes quickly
Hydrocarbon; it interacts least with the polar stationary phase, so it spends the most time in the mobile phase
All three travel together (same Rf) because polarity is irrelevant in TLC
Carboxylic acid; it has the largest molecular weight so it diffuses fastest
ochem.why: On polar silica, the LEAST polar compound interacts least with the stationary phase and is carried farthest by the non-polar mobile phase. Hydrocarbon → highest Rf; carboxylic acid (most polar) → lowest Rf.

ochem.q: Compare the relative rates of E2 elimination for three substrates with the same alkyl-halide skeleton: 1-bromobutane, 2-bromobutane, and 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, with concentrated KOC(CH₃)₃ in t-butanol. Rank by E2 rate (fastest first).
opts: 3° > 2° > 1° (more β-H availability and more stable alkene products)
ochem.why: Bulky base strongly favors E2. Rate increases with substrate substitution: more β-H positions and the resulting alkene is more substituted (more stable). 3° > 2° > 1°. The bulky base also suppresses competing SN2.

ochem.q: Phenol is brominated with Br₂ in water (no Lewis acid needed) to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol. Why does this aromatic substrate require neither FeBr₃ nor any other Lewis-acid catalyst, and why does TRI-bromination occur in a single reaction even though aromatic rings normally over-substitute only on activated rings?
opts: Phenol is highly activated; the OH lone pair donates strongly into the ring, generating sufficient electrophile (Br⁺) reactivity without a Lewis acid. Each successive Br adds activation, leading to 2,4,6-tribromination
Phenol is deactivated; tribromination is anomalous
Water acts as the Lewis acid catalyst
Phenol carries a net negative charge in water
Br₂ rapidly hydrolyses to HOBr, which alone can brominate
ochem.why: OH is a strong activator (resonance donor). The ring is electron-rich enough that polarized Br–Br cleaves heterolytically without Lewis-acid help. Each substitution still leaves a strongly activated ring, so substitution proceeds 2× more (ortho and para available) until the 2,4,6 positions are all brominated.

ochem.q: When propanoic acid reacts with thionyl chloride (SOCl₂), then ammonia, then heat with P₂O₅ to dehydrate, the final product is a nitrile. Identify the nitrile and explain why each step is needed.
opts: Propanenitrile (CH₃CH₂CN); SOCl₂ activates COOH → acid chloride; NH₃ converts to primary amide; P₂O₅ dehydrates amide to nitrile
Acetonitrile (CH₃CN) — one carbon is lost during dehydration
Hydrocyanic acid (HCN); the propyl chain is lost
ochem.why: COOH → COCl (SOCl₂) → CONH₂ (NH₃) → CN (dehydration with P₂O₅). Three carbons retained: propanenitrile.
